They're their own globals, not part of global.config, because "init config defaults" takes frigate_camera out of each entry before the config is stored: in Node-RED, Frigate's name lives only in frigate_cameras, camera_labels, and the frigate_facts flow context on capture-events, where "keep frigate facts" keeps each camera's detect size from Frigate's /api/config under Frigate's name. Only two nodes read an event before its camera gets the key: "vet sub_label" and "frigate fields", which looks the detect size up by Frigate's name and puts no name in what it adds. "append config" then looks each event's camera up in frigate_cameras and sets it to the key, so the events row, tm/event and tm/events, ThingsBoard, and Plate Recognizer carry only the key. An event from a camera the map lacks is dropped with one warning, and a camera_radar that names no radar records the event without one.

docs.title: The Network module and the hotspot
docs.text:
The network module adds the Network check group (hotspot, wifi, internet, and wifi_country, in modules/network/checks.py) and the Network page's routes. Both read the unit's network through adapters/network.py, which runs nmcli and iw and never asks for a secret. An offline unit is normal, so the Internet check is never a warning or an error, and a read that fails is unknown. The hotspot's values come from the manifest's network section. The checks' words are the contract with the operator page.

The routes are in modules/network/router.py:

Route Who What it does GET /network Any signed-in user The unit's names, its Ethernet and Wi-Fi links (MAC and IP addresses, gateway, DNS servers), the internet, and the hotspot's state, as NetworkState from state.py. A value NetworkManager doesn't give is missing, not an error, and readable: false says it didn't answer at all. It never holds a password. GET /network/hotspot/password Admins The password file's text, "" for a hotspot with no password, and null when the file can't be read. The answer carries Cache-Control: no-store, and each call records a network.hotspot_password_shown audit row. It is the only place a password leaves the device. POST /network/hotspot Admins Takes any of enabled, name, password, and hidden, checks them, and answers 202 with the job's id. A name takes 1 to 32 bytes of UTF-8 and a password 8 to 63 printable ASCII characters, each with no space at either end; a value that breaks its rule, or a request with nothing to change, is a 422 with a sentence and no job. A unit with no hotspot profile is a 409 (no_hotspot). The audit row network.hotspot lists the fields sent, never their values.

The Wi-Fi routes come from modules/network/wifi.py and the same router. wifi.py reads three files that root's scripts write in /run/traffic-monitor/ (network-scan.json, network-retry.json, and network-join.json) and the saved networks from adapters/network.py. It is read only and never reads a password. A file that is missing, unreadable, or not in its form reads as nothing, not as an error. NetworkManager's sentences are never read: a saved network is what saved_wifi returns, and the network in use is its profile's UUID. The profile a join is testing is left out of the saved networks until the join saves it, because NetworkManager lists it while the test runs.

Route Who What it does GET /network/wifi Any signed-in user WifiNetworks: the saved networks in the order the unit tries them (with in_use, automatic, hidden, in_range, and could_not_join), the nearby networks from the last scan (with signal, security, saved, in_use), how long ago the scan was, and the join. GET /network/join Any signed-in user The JoinState the Network page's card and the home page's banner show, or null. It reads one file, and the join unit's state while a stage is still going: a pending stage while the unit isn't running reads as interrupted. POST /network/wifi/scan Admin Starts the network job's scan. A radio that is missing (no_radio) or off (radio_off) is a 409 before any job. POST /network/wifi/forget Admin Starts forget for a saved network's UUID, or 404 for one that isn't saved. The audit row names the network. POST /network/wifi/order Admin Starts order with the UUIDs of exactly the networks that join by themselves, or 409 stale_order. POST /network/wifi/join Admin Checks the name and password, the radio, that no join is pending, that the network isn't in use, and that the last scan heard it with a password; then starts the network-join job with a name and password, or a saved network's UUID when no password is sent. The audit row names the network and holds no password. POST /network/wifi/join/switch Admin Starts the network job's switch-now, or 409 no_countdown. POST /network/wifi/join/cancel Admin Starts cancel, which also dismisses a result. 409 while the join is switching.

Every route that starts a change refuses it with 409 join_pending while a join is testing, counting down, or switching (refuse_while_joining), and the Network page disables its controls the same way. The routes answer 202 with the job's id and the page follows the job with GET /jobs/{id}. In fake mode, fake_network stands in for NetworkManager, the password file, and the join job's state.

jobs/tm-job-network is the root script behind POST /network/hotspot, run by tm-job-network.service. Its docstring lists every check and the order of its steps. The request is {"action": "hotspot"} plus the fields that were sent. The script repeats the name and password rules from router.py, because it imports nothing from tm-control, and a test keeps the two the same. In short, it:

  1. Checks the request, then takes the lock, /run/traffic-monitor/network.lock. tm-network-retry takes the same lock, so the timer never moves the radio in the middle of a change. The job waits for it up to 10 seconds, and the retry run, which never waits, prints locked and stops.
  2. Writes a new password to the password file first, and then changes the profile with one nmcli connection modify. The file is the source of truth, so a failed change puts the old file back.
  3. Restarts the hotspot only when it is up and its name, password, or hidden setting changed (connection up applies them). Turning the hotspot off takes it down. Turning it on, on the built-in radio only, switches the radio on if it is off and starts the hotspot if the radio is idle. Nothing here restarts NetworkManager.

It prints one line per step, never a password, and exits 1 with refused: <sentence> or failed: <step>; a line ending the settings are saved means the profile changed and only the restart failed.

tm-job-network has five more actions, {"action": "scan"}, forget, order, switch-now, and cancel, and the same checks, hostile request, and lock. Its docstring has the full list:

  • scan runs iw dev <device> scan flush and writes network-scan.json: the time, and each network heard with its signal (0 to 100) and its security (open, password, wpa3, enterprise, or other). What iw prints is the names and settings of other people's networks, so the script parses it as text, never prints it, and sends a name to nmcli only when tm-control sends it back in a later request. flush empties the kernel's cache first, because a plain scan keeps listing a network for about 30 seconds after it left the air. While iw is busy (exit status 240, which it is while NetworkManager scans and for 10 to 14 seconds after the hotspot restarts) the action tries again every 5 seconds for as long as its 60 seconds last.
  • forget deletes a saved Wi-Fi client profile by UUID. When the unit was on it, it waits for the radio and starts the hotspot if nothing took over.
  • order gives the networks that join by themselves a priority, the first the highest, changing only the ones that differ.
  • switch-now and cancel never wait for the lock, because the join job holds it for its whole run. They write one word to network-join.control, which the join job reads every second. cancel on a finished result removes the state file, and on a join that died it rolls back the checkpoint, deletes the profile under test unless it is saved, and then removes the state file.

docs.title: The Wi-Fi join
docs.text:
jobs/tm-job-network-join is the root script behind POST /network/wifi/join, run by tm-job-network-join.service. Its request is {"ssid": ..., "password": ...} or {"uuid": ...}, and it deletes the request as soon as it reads it, so the password is on /run for a moment. Its docstring lists every step. In short, it:

  1. Takes the lock and holds it to the end. Held by someone else: the state becomes failed with reason busy. When the state file shows that an earlier run died mid-test, the job rolls back that run's checkpoint and deletes its profile under test unless it is saved. A checkpoint that no such run left belongs to another program, such as Cockpit's networking page around each change, so the job leaves it alone; step 3 then fails, and nothing is changed.
  2. Checks the radio and the profile in use, and scans with flush, once; a scan that fails doesn't stop the test. A network the scan doesn't hear is failed with reason not_in_range, and the radio is never touched. The flush is what keeps the hotspot from being taken away for a network that has just left.
  3. Makes the checkpoint: a NetworkManager checkpoint with a 90-second rollback timeout, over D-Bus with busctl. If it can't, the job stops before it touches the radio. After this point every path, including an error and SIGTERM, rolls back to the checkpoint. If the script itself dies, NetworkManager rolls back by itself 90 seconds later.
  4. Adds the profile under test in memory (save no), so a password that fails never reaches the microSD card, and runs nmcli --wait 45 connection up on it. The in-memory profile is the only place the new password lives, and the job never prints it.
  5. On success reads the address and DNS servers and probes the internet: up to three DNS questions, a second apart, to the network's first two DNS servers in turn (the first question right after a join can fail at once), then one HTTP request to connectivity-check.ubuntu.com, over sockets bound to the Wi-Fi, in 10 seconds in all. Only the answer's status code is read: 204 is reachable, and any other answer is sign_in_page. No address, no answer, or an error is not_reachable.
  6. Rolls back the checkpoint and waits for the radio to be where it was. A failure is not_joined, or no_address when the join waited out its 45 seconds with the device connected but without an address (exit status 3 with the device at state 70).
  7. Counts down 300 seconds, reading the control file every second. cancel ends it and deletes the profile unless it is saved. switch starts the switch.
  8. Switches: sets the profile to autoconnect with a priority above every other saved network, deletes the saved profiles of the same name when the password is new, and runs connection up. The radio is read until it is up on any profile. If it isn't, connection up on the profile it was on, or on the hotspot, and the state is switch_failed; the network stays saved and its failure goes on record in network-retry.json.

The reasons the page gives come from the scan and from exit statuses and device states, never from a sentence of nmcli, iw, or busctl, which can carry a command line. The job prints fixed sentences, exit statuses, and error type names.

The files, all in /run/traffic-monitor/, 0644 and root's, each written under a temporary name and renamed:

File Written by Holds network-scan.json tm-job-network (scan) The networks heard, strongest first, with the time. network-join.json tm-job-network-join The state: stage (testing, countdown, switching, joined, failed, cancelled, switch_failed), ssid, uuid, saved, before, joined, reason (not_in_range, not_joined, no_address, busy, error), address, internet, switch_monotonic, finished_at. Never the password. tm-control adds interrupted when a pending stage's unit isn't running. network-join.control tm-job-network (switch-now, cancel) One word, switch or cancel. The join job reads it every second and removes it once read, and whenever a run ends. network-retry.json tm-network-retry, and the join job for a failure The failures on record per saved network, which set its wait of 5, 15, then 60 minutes.

The lock, /run/traffic-monitor/network.lock, is held by tm-job-network for its run, by tm-job-network-join for all of its run (the test, the countdown, and the switch), and by each tm-network-retry run. The retry never waits for it, so the timer never moves the radio mid-change. tm-job-network waits up to 10 seconds, except for switch-now and cancel, which must reach a join that holds it. A join that finds the lock held ends as busy.

The unit allows 900 seconds (TimeoutStartSec), the longest a run can take: 10 + 60 + 90 + 45 + 300 + 75 + 45. TimeoutStopSec=120 gives a stop time to roll back.

Two scripts in jobs/ run as root, and neither is a tm-job unit. Both are standard-library Python with no tm_control imports, run as /usr/bin/python3 -EP from the root-owned /usr/local/libexec/traffic-monitor/, and read no password into their output:

Script Run by What it does tm-hotspot-setup The installer's wifi tasks Creates the tm-hotspot profile, or adopts an access-point profile made by hand, and ensures its device, priority, mode, address, and IPv6 setting. The password file is the source of truth for the password. It never activates or deactivates a profile, so a joined phone stays joined. Its docstring lists the order of its steps and its exit statuses. tm-network-retry tm-network-retry.timer, 90 seconds after boot and 5 minutes after each run ends, and the Hotspot check's Restart the hotspot Keeps the radio on a known network or on the hotspot. It starts the hotspot when no network holds the radio, leaves it alone while a phone is joined, and scans for the saved networks otherwise, one network per run, with a 5, 15, then 60 minute wait after each failure. Its docstring lists its steps and outcomes. It keeps its memory in /run/traffic-monitor/network-retry.json.

tm-hotspot-firewall.service loads the inet tm_hotspot nftables table before NetworkManager can start the hotspot. The table drops forwarded traffic into and out of the hotspot's subnet, so phones on it reach the unit and nothing behind it.

nginx's sign-in rule is in container/revproxy/nginx.conf.j2. On the hotspot dnsmasq answers every name with the unit's address, so a phone's connection test arrives with a foreign Host. A request that arrived on the hotspot's address with any name but that address or the unit's own is redirected to http://10.42.0.1/, which makes the phone open its sign-in window. The rule must never answer such a test with success: on Android 17 no browser reaches the unit until its user allows the Nearby devices permission for it, so the sign-in window is the only way in that needs no setup. nginx also sets X-TM-Hotspot: 1 from the address a request arrived on, replacing any value the client sent, and GET /api/v1/setup/status then returns hotspot.local_name, which the login and setup pages show in a note: the address to copy, and the steps from a phone's sign-in window to a browser. The same answer carries hostname for everyone, with no login, and the control app's tab and bar take the unit's name from it, so the pages before login name the unit too. The name is no secret: mDNS announces it on the network.

sudo tm-control card (core/card.py) prints the device's addresses, the hotspot's name and password, and the setup code. It refuses to run without root, reads the password and setup-code files and nmcli's answer first, and only then opens the state database. --json prints the same values, and --unclaimed-only, which the installer passes, prints nothing and exits 3 once the device is claimed.

docs.title: What the sandbox allows
docs.text:
tm-control.service runs with ProtectSystem=strict, RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_NETLINK, and SupplementaryGroups=systemd-journal video. It writes its state and runtime directories and two config directories under the code directory (ReadWritePaths): Frigate's, frigate/config, for the models the Detection page manages, and Node-RED's, node-red-tm/config, for the config.yml the Location page writes. The rest of the system is read-only to it. The sandbox also shaped the probes:

  • The Coral USB check reads the vendor and product ids from /sys/bus/usb/devices rather than running lsusb, which needed a netlink socket the service first lacked, and ss falls back to reading /proc/net for the MQTT broker's port.
  • AF_NETLINK is there for iw, which reads the Wi-Fi country for the Network checks. The Network checks otherwise use nmcli, which needs nothing more, and never ask it for a password.
  • vcgencmd get_throttled needs the video group to open /dev/vcio_gencmd. Without it, the power check says to rerun the installer.
  • The HEVC decoder check compares /dev/rpi-hevc-dec with the media device whose /sys/bus/media/devices/mediaN/model names the decoder.
  • timedatectl show prints its times as local strings; tm-control reads the clock itself.
  • tm-control never writes the secrets directory; the set-secret and network jobs do. It reads the hotspot's password file (mode 0640, the secrets directory's group) for the one admin-only route.

docs.title: Keeping the credits current
docs.text:
The About page lists the open source projects the device is built on. Its list is one file, tm-control/ui/src/modules/about/credits.json, with a row for each project: its name, license type, address, the group it is shown in, and sometimes a short note. The two rows in the group built-on (Frigate NVR and Node-RED) also have a sentence in does, which the page shows under "Built on".

The list credits only what Traffic Monitor names itself, not what those projects bring with them:

  • the direct dependencies of the control app's pages (tm-control/ui/package.json), of its backend (tm-control/backend/requirements.txt), and of Node-RED (container/node-red-tm/data/package.json);
  • the components the installer records in the manifest (components in the role's tm-control_service.yml), such as Frigate, go2rtc, and nginx;
  • a few things the installer puts on the unit by name, such as FFmpeg, Podman, and Cockpit.

Each row's covers list says which dependencies and components the row answers for, as ui:<npm name>, node-red:<npm name>, python:<pip name>, or component:<manifest key>. A row with no covers is one the test can't check.

script/tests/test_about_credits.py fails when a dependency or a component has no row, and when a row answers for something that is gone. Its message names each one, so it tells you what to add or remove. To add a row, copy the license type from the project's own license file, not from a package listing, and use the project's own page as the address. If the project states no license, ask the maintainer rather than guessing. Open the address to check that it works.

The test can't see these, so look them over before a release:

  • the apt packages in the role's vars/main.yml, and whether a package is worth a row (a new service or a new tool the installer relies on);
  • the Containerfiles, for the video tools they build, FFmpeg and its encoders (x264 and x265) among them, and the license each is built under;
  • the Coral model and where it comes from. Its row gives YOLOv9's license, GPL-3.0, and not the MIT license of the repository that publishes the model: a unit holds only the model file and its labels, the model is built from YOLOv9, and its release states no license of its own. If a later release states one, use that;
  • the map source (tmsetup_map_style_url), and the credit the page gives for it;
  • the sentence about trademarks, which names each trademark's owner. Add a name when a new project's name appears on the page, and keep to naming projects, never showing their logos.

The same page links to third-party-licenses.txt, the license texts of the libraries bundled into the control app's pages. The UI build makes it (build.license in tm-control/ui/vite.config.ts) and writes it to dist/. It is generated, so never edit it or add it to git.

docs.title: Run it on a laptop
docs.text:
Fake mode runs the whole app without a Pi: it uses the test manifest, fixed secrets that aren't secret, a job runner that pretends, a clock in memory for the Date and time page, a status report from tests/fixtures/status_fake.json, whose groups show every status and kind of fix, a fake Node-RED for the Location page, and a fake Frigate with a second camera, oak_ave_tele, that no entry in the seeded config.yml points at, so the Cameras page's actions work. Its state goes in ./.tm-control-fake/. From the repository root, in the dev environment from Contributing:

TM_CONTROL_FAKE=1 PYTHONPATH=tm-control/backend python -m tm_control fake-reset   # an unclaimed device; prints its setup code
TM_CONTROL_FAKE=1 PYTHONPATH=tm-control/backend python -m tm_control serve        # the backend on 127.0.0.1:8090
cd tm-control/ui && npm ci && npm run dev                                         # the UI on http://localhost:5173

Fake mode seeds .tm-control-fake/node-red-tm/config/config.yml from tests/fixtures/node_red_config_ok.yml (a camera and a radar, and a deployment block at 45.0, -122.0 with no survey id), and keeps it, with whatever the app wrote to it, until the next fake-reset. Its Node-RED (FakeNodeRed in fake.py) keeps deployment rows in memory and runs the deployment engine's rules on them whenever that file changes, so deploys, corrections, and hand edits of the file behave as on a device; after a restart of serve, only the place in use has deployments. It has no traffic to count, so an open camera or radar row counts as having recorded traffic 30 seconds after it starts (RECORDS_AFTER), which is what lets the Mounting save's question come up on a laptop. Its backup directory is empty, so there's nothing to import. Fake mode also seeds .tm-control-fake/model_cache with two synthetic model pairs and the installer's model file, and keeps the model its fake Frigate runs in .tm-control-fake/running-model; Use there changes that file and restarts nothing. The fake Frigate can download one Frigate+ model ID, fedcba9876543210fedcba9876543210 (fake.FAKE_FETCHABLE_ID); any other ID is refused after 5 seconds (FAKE_FETCH_SECONDS), as a device would show a refusal. The Frigate+ key has to be set first, or the route answers 409 no_key. In fake mode the API's interactive docs are at /api/v1/docs. tm-control/ui/README.md has the commands for building and testing the UI in the same Node image the device uses.

Every change to the API regenerates the UI's typed client in the same commit, so each commit's tests pass:

PYTHONPATH=tm-control/backend python -m tm_control dump-openapi > tm-control/ui/src/api/openapi.json
(cd tm-control/ui && npm run api:generate)   # writes src/api/schema.d.ts

Run the backend's tests with the rest of the off-device tests:

.venv/bin/python -m pytest tm-control/backend/tests script/tests container/node-red-tm/schema/tests

docs.title: Add a module
docs.text:
A feature is one backend module and, if it has pages, one UI module.

  1. Backend: add backend/tm_control/modules/<name>/ with a router.py (an APIRouter) and an __init__.py that makes module = Module("<name>", router), with check_groups= if it has status checks. Add it to MODULES in modules/__init__.py. Endpoints take current_user or require_admin from modules/auth/deps.py, and raise ApiError for anything the operator should see.
  2. State: if it needs tables, add the next migration in core/state.py.
  3. UI: add ui/src/modules/<name>/ with its pages and an index.ts that lists its routes and menu entries, and add it to ui/src/modules/index.ts. Regenerate the typed client as the UI's README describes.
  4. Root work: prefer a polkit action or unit verb on the list. Otherwise add the job's name to JOB_NAMES in core/jobs.py, its script to tm-control/jobs/, its unit to the role's templates/tm-control/, and the unit to the polkit list.
  5. A new app behind the login: add its location file with an auth snippet to container/revproxy/tm/locations/ and to tmsetup_revproxy_locations, and its tile to APPS in modules/system/router.py and to ui/src/modules/home/apps.ts. An app on its own port, as Cockpit is on 9090, has no location file: its APPS row has None for the file and its port, and the tile links to that port on the name the browser used.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: A Traffic Monitor is a Raspberry Pi 5 running a few cooperating programs. Everything happens on the device, so it works without an internet connection once it's installed.

docs.title: From the street to the database
docs.text:
1. The camera streams H.265 video at 1536×864 and 10 frames per second to Frigate.
  2. Frigate finds and tracks objects in the video, using the AI accelerator if the device has one and the CPU if not. It records which zones each object passed through. When an object leaves the frame, Frigate publishes an event on the device's MQTT broker.
  3. The radar (optional) measures the speed and direction of whatever moves in front of it and reports readings over USB several times a second.

  4. Node-RED runs the Traffic Monitor logic. It keeps every radar reading, and it records every moving object from an enabled camera as an event, with the path it took across the picture. When the object entered any zone, it:

    • works out the direction of travel from the order in which the object entered zone_near and zone_far, or from the camera's radar if the zones don't give one;
    • attaches a speed: the median radar reading in that direction while the object was in view, with a two-second margin on each side, or Frigate's own estimate when the radar gives none.

    Without a radar, the direction comes from the zones, and a speed only from Frigate, which estimates one only in a zone you set up for it. Direction and speed has the exact rules.

    The dashboards and the daily counts then filter the events by zone: they count objects that passed through zone_capture, and they use only objects that passed through zone_radar for speed statistics. 5. The database, one SQLite file on the device, stores the events, the radar readings, air quality readings from the optional sensor, and the device's deployment history. The dashboards read from it, and you can download it.

First-time setup walks through turning on detection and adjusting the four zones. Events lists every column an event has.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text: The device serves a home page at http://<device>/ that links to the dashboards, Frigate, and the system tools. Home page and apps describes each one.

docs.title: What stays on the device
docs.text: The database holds labels, times, speeds, and zones, not pictures. Frigate keeps cropped snapshots and short clips for about an hour so you can check what was detected, and nothing is sent anywhere unless you turn on an integration. Data and privacy has the details.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Three files on the device control the behavior described above. You edit them over SSH.

File What it controls Frigate's config.yml Camera, detection, zones, object filters, and recording. Most changes are made in Frigate's own web UI. See Tune object detection. Node-RED's config.yml Deployment location, which sensors are on, which radar pairs with which camera, and the ThingsBoard connection. Times shown on the dashboards use the device's time zone, which the installer sets and the control app's Date and time page changes. See config.yml settings. node-red-tm.env Radar serial ports, the database path, and the MQTT broker. See node-red-tm.env settings.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The dashboard shows no counts

Follow the checklist in First-time setup. The usual causes, in order: detection is off in Frigate, the objects don't pass through zone_capture, or the camera isn't enabled in config.yml.

Counts, but no speeds

The radar must be enabled in config.yml and named in the camera's camera_radar, zone_radar must cover the road, and the device must be at a shallow angle to the traffic. If the radar was plugged in after the software was installed, rerun bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm so the container can see it.

Frigate shows no camera image

Open Camera feeds from the home page, logged in as the administrator. If the picam_h265_detect stream plays there, the camera and its stream work, and the fault is between Frigate and the stream. Either the camera is off in Frigate's configuration editor, where cameras: picam_h265: needs enabled: true, or Frigate's video decoding is failing, which shows as ffmpeg errors in the frigate.service log. If the stream doesn't play, check the camera cable, then look at the go2rtc_server.service log in System administration.

Detection is slow or misses objects

Without an AI accelerator, Frigate detects on the CPU and can't keep up with a busy road. Hardware lists the supported accelerators. If you added one after installing, see Add an accelerator later. With an accelerator, see Tune object detection.

The home page opens on a computer but not on an Android phone

On Android 17, an app needs the Nearby devices permission to reach anything on the phone's own Wi-Fi network. Despite its name, the permission covers the local network. A browser without it times out on every device there, including your router's page and a Traffic Monitor on its own hotspot, while computers reach the device. Allow it once for each browser you use:

  1. On the phone, open Settings > Apps and choose the browser.
  2. Choose Permissions > Nearby devices > Allow.
  3. Open the device's address again.

Chrome asks for the permission when you open a device's address and takes you to its App info page, where step 2 is the same. In Firefox, follow the steps yourself. Android's local network protection page describes the permission.

On the device's own hotspot, the phone's sign-in window opens the control app without the permission, and a browser needs one more step: keeping the network. See Wi-Fi and the hotspot.

The hotspot doesn't show up on my phone

If its name is hidden, the phone doesn't list it. On Android, choose Add network, type the name, and tick Hidden network. See Hide the name.

The first install seems stuck

Building Frigate's container image compiles ffmpeg on the device, which takes about 20 minutes with little output. Leave it running. The whole first install takes 30 minutes or more.

A database download fails

See Data export.

The Status page says the database schema is behind

Each time Node-RED starts, it updates the database's tables to the version the installed software expects. If an update fails, it's undone, and Node-RED runs on the old tables, where it may not be able to save new data. To see why it failed, run this over SSH or in Cockpit's terminal:

sudo journalctl -u node-red-tm | grep tmdb-migrate

If Node-RED started recently, the diagnostics on the Device page show the same lines. Restarting Node-RED tries the update again. If it fails again, ask for help and attach the diagnostics.

I edited config.yml and nothing changed

The Traffic Monitor reads the file again when you save it, so a change that doesn't take effect usually means a YAML error, such as a wrong indent or a missing space after a colon. The node-red-tm.service log in System administration shows the error. Fix the file before you restart the service; config.yml settings explains why.

docs.title: What does the device record?
docs.text: The database records what passed (a label such as car), when, how fast, and through which zones. It holds no images and no plate numbers with the default settings. Frigate keeps a cropped snapshot and a short clip of each detection for about an hour, so you can check what it saw, and you can turn that off. By default, the device sends no images or video anywhere: everything is processed on the device, and the database holds only metadata. It uploads nothing until an administrator turns on sharing. The live view, the recordings, and Frigate's snapshots are behind the device's login, which decides who on your network can open the apps. It isn't a control on the images themselves: anyone with an account can see them, and they're ordinary files on the device's card. Data and privacy explains, and lists the features that would change what's stored.

docs.title: Why this design?
docs.text:
The Traffic Monitor is built privacy-first because we believe in:

  • Ethical and transparent monitoring. The code, the architecture, and the models are open, so anyone can see what the device does, and operators, especially public bodies, can be held to account.
  • Community safety and trust. Detection runs on the device, nothing is sent to an outside server unless you set it up, and the data stays in your control.
  • Unbiased data collection. Detection runs without human bias, but machine learning models can carry algorithmic bias. We use public-domain and open source models wherever possible and name the models in use.

To keep an area out of view, aim the camera so the area is out of frame. A motion mask doesn't hide it; see Data and privacy.

docs.title: How many objects can it track at once?
docs.text:
More than a busy street produces. The practical limit is objects hiding each other, as at the start of a race, where the camera can't see the person behind another.

The AI accelerator runs an inference in about 10 ms, which is about 100 inferences per second, and Frigate runs several inferences per frame when there's motion in several places. On a road with trees casting moving shadows, Frigate has been seen checking more than 18 motion regions and tracking 9 labeled objects at once, with inference time still around 9 ms. The video is decoded in hardware, and the CPU, which encodes the camera stream and runs motion detection, had headroom to spare. Frigate's discussions #7491 and #18326 explain how detections per frame are bounded.

A road where shadows produce many motion regions, all checked for objects

docs.title: Ideas and use cases
docs.text: The device collects more than counts. With extra zones in Frigate and the event data, you can study how people and vehicles interact. Three examples follow; share yours in Show and tell.

docs.title: Near misses at a crosswalk
docs.text:
A near miss is a driver and a vulnerable road user, such as a pedestrian at a crosswalk, in conflict at the same moment. These events are rarely captured today. The first step is a definition, and traffic law supplies one. As an example, Oregon's rules, summarized by Portland Bicycle School:

  • Every corner is a crosswalk (ORS 801.220).
  • A pedestrian has claimed the crossing as soon as any part of them, or their cane, wheelchair, or bicycle, enters it (ORS 811.028(4), 814.040(1)(a)).
  • A driver must stay stopped until the pedestrian has cleared the driver's lane, or the lane they're turning into, plus one more lane (ORS 811.028).

To capture conflicts:

  1. Mount the device with a view of the whole intersection.
  2. Draw zones for the pedestrian areas and the driver areas.
  3. Each person and car event then records its start_time, end_time, and entered_zones.
  4. Download the data and look for a car entering a driver zone while a person was in the conflicting pedestrian zone.

For example, a person in zone_ped_ne about to cross south or west, and a car that enters zone_intersection_e and turns into zone_intersection_n before the person has crossed, is a near miss or at least an illegal turn. You can tighten the definition further: was the car stationary at the stop sign first, or did a pedestrian zone at the very edge of the sidewalk show intent to cross? A person and a car in the same road zone at the same time is the most serious case.

Zones for a near-miss study: pedestrian zones on each corner and intersection zones on each approach

docs.title: Vehicles that don't stop at a stop sign
docs.text:
A rolling stop, also called a California stop or Rhode Island stop, is a vehicle that passes a stop sign without stopping fully or for the required time. Some places let cyclists treat a stop sign as a yield (the Idaho stop).

  1. Mount the device high, looking down at the whole intersection.

  2. In Frigate, draw a thin stop-sign zone across the road just before each stop sign, such as zone_stop_sign_e and zone_stop_sign_w for a two-way stop.

  3. Give each stop-sign zone a loitering time that matches your jurisdiction, such as 3 seconds, and limit it to car if you like. The zone then appears in an event's entered_zones only if the vehicle stayed in it that long. A vehicle that rolled through has an event without the zone.

  4. Optionally add wider zones for each approach, so you can also see turning movements: a car that went from zone_intersection_e to zone_intersection_n turned right.

  5. Check the zones against a few real vehicles in Frigate's Explore view. It can take a while to find a car that stops properly.

docs.title: Without a loitering time
docs.text:
A second way needs no time chosen in advance. Give the stop-sign zone no loitering time and no side lengths for speed estimation. Every vehicle's event then has its seconds in the zone in zone_times, and how many of them it was stationary, so you can try one, two, or three seconds afterwards against the same events. Time stopped and time in each zone has an example query.

Frigate's stationary flag is no help at a stop sign: it marks an object stationary only after about ten seconds without moving, which a full stop rarely lasts. The time in the zone is what to compare. A zone with a loitering time records only the time beyond it.

docs.title: How long vehicles stay parked
docs.text:
1. In Frigate, draw a zone over the parking bays, such as zone_parking, without side lengths for speed estimation.
  2. A vehicle that parks and leaves is one event, saved when it leaves. Its zone_times has its time in the bay and how much of that it was stationary.

For a 15-minute bay, the vehicles that stayed longer than allowed are the events with more than 900 seconds stationary in the zone:

SELECT id,
       datetime(start_time, 'unixepoch', 'localtime') AS arrived,
       json_extract(zone_times, '$.zone_parking.stationary') AS seconds_parked
FROM events
WHERE json_extract(zone_times, '$.zone_parking.stationary') > 900
ORDER BY start_time;

The limits:

  • Six hours is the most a figure says; 21600 means six hours or more.
  • A vehicle that is still parked has no event yet.
  • A vehicle that was already parked when the device or Frigate started is timed only from then.
  • If Frigate loses sight of a parked vehicle and finds it again, as when a passing vehicle hides it for a moment, the stay is split into two or more events, each shorter than the stay, and a part can be missing. A vehicle that stayed longer than allowed can then have no event over the limit.

docs.title: description: Where to ask questions, report bugs, and share ideas: the chat, GitHub discussions, and issues.
Get support
docs.text: The Traffic Monitor is a volunteer-run open source project. The community answers questions as it can, so please be patient, and help others when you can. Everyone follows the Code of Conduct.

docs.title: Search first
docs.text: Search these docs, then the repository: the search box at the top right covers discussions, issues, and code, with filters on the left.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text: The Traffic Monitor Zulip chat is the quickest place to ask a question, suggest an idea, or show a deployment. Developers discuss code there too, so it's also the place to start contributing.

docs.title: GitHub discussions
docs.text:
The discussions board is for longer conversations:

  • 💬 General: anything at all
  • 💡 Ideas: feature ideas, and votes on them
  • 🗳️ Polls
  • 🙏 Q&A: ask for help
  • 👐 Show and tell: what you've built

docs.title: GitHub issues
docs.text:
Open an issue for a specific bug, or for a feature request with an idea of how it should work. A feature idea with no design yet goes to Ideas, above. Include enough detail for someone else to reproduce or understand it.

  • 🐞 Bug report
  • 💡 Feature request

An issue may be closed without a full resolution, for example as a duplicate, after inactivity, or because the work is tracked elsewhere. That isn't a lack of interest; comment or reopen if it still matters.

docs.title: Report a security problem
docs.text: If you find a way for someone to get into a Traffic Monitor, read its data, or take it over without permission, report it privately through the repository's security page, not in an issue, a discussion, or the chat. SECURITY.md says what to include.

docs.title: Network ports
docs.text:
Other computers reach the Traffic Monitor's apps through the home page on port 80. The apps themselves, and the control app on port 8090, listen only on the device itself (loopback). The ports in the table below are the ones other computers can reach.

Port Used for 22 SSH 80 The control app and every app behind its login 1883 MQTT, only when the broker has a login. See MQTT and ThingsBoard. 5353 (UDP) <hostname>.local names (mDNS) 8554 The camera stream (RTSP), with a username and password 9090 Cockpit, with your Raspberry Pi login. The home page's Cockpit tile opens it, and it works when the home page doesn't.

docs.title: The hotspot
docs.text:
When the device's Wi-Fi isn't on a network it knows, it runs a hotspot on the built-in radio (wlan0). The control app's Network page shows the device's own addresses.

Address The device is 10.42.0.1, on the network 10.42.0.0/24. The address is fixed. DHCP The device gives each phone an address in that network. DNS The device answers every name with its own address, so a phone's connection test lands on the device and opens the control app's sign-in window. Ports The same as on your network, in the table above. Reach A phone on the hotspot reaches only the device. A firewall rule drops anything that would pass from the hotspot to another network, or back, so the hotspot has no internet and doesn't open your wired network to a phone.

A request that reaches the device on the hotspot's address with any other name, such as the one a phone's connection test uses, gets a redirect to http://10.42.0.1/. A request for 10.42.0.1 or for the device's own name is answered as usual.

Whenever the device has a network, NetworkManager asks connectivity-check.ubuntu.com every 5 minutes whether the internet is reachable. The Status page's Internet check shows the answer. When an administrator tests a Wi-Fi network from the Network page, the device asks that network's DNS server for the address of connectivity-check.ubuntu.com (up to three times, a second apart) and makes one request to it through that network, to report whether the internet is reachable there.

docs.title: Camera stream login
docs.text:
The camera stream on port 8554 needs the username frigate and a password generated on the device at install. To play the stream in another program, such as VLC, read the password on the device:

sudo cat /etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/go2rtc_rtsp_password

Then open rtsp://frigate:<password>@<device>:8554/picam_h265_detect.

docs.title: Installer options
docs.text:
script/tmsetup.sh in the repository installs and updates the Traffic Monitor. Run it from the device, or from another computer with -H. Install the software and Update the software show the usual runs.

bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh [flags]

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Meaning -h Show the usage text and exit. -y Answer yes to every prompt, including the reboot. -v Verbose output. Repeat for more. -f Replace the user-editable settings files with fresh copies from the templates. See What -f replaces. -t TAG Run one component, plus anything that has to change with it. Repeat for several. See Tags. -T List the tags and exit. -C NAME[,NAME] Turn on an optional component: plate_recognizer (see Plate Recognizer), or mqtt_lan, which creates an MQTT broker login when there isn't one (see Connect from other devices). -u Also upgrade the operating system's packages (apt full-upgrade). -d PATH Install folder. Default /opt/traffic-monitor. The docs assume the default. -o USER Owner of the installed files and processes. Default tmadmin, created by the installer. -g GROUP Group of the installed files. Default tmadmin. -w CODE The Wi-Fi country, a two-letter code such as US or GB. Without it, the installer asks when the device has none and the run includes the wifi tag; with -y or a remote run it keeps the device's country, or sets US when there is none. See The Wi-Fi country. -z TIMEZONE Time zone for the system and the dashboards, as a tz database name. Default America/Los_Angeles. -L PATH Where to write the installer's log. -a ARG Pass an extra argument to the underlying Ansible run, without its leading hyphen.

Remote runs:

Flag Meaning -H HOST[,HOST] Install to these devices over SSH instead of the local machine. Separate several with commas. The computer you run it from needs Python 3.12 or later, for the installer's Ansible. -l USER The SSH username on the devices. -k Ask for the SSH password. -K Ask for the password for administrator rights (sudo). Needed on Raspberry Pi OS unless you've set up passwordless sudo.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Each tag reruns one part of the install. Without -t, everything runs. The pod, the reverse proxy, and the control app that checks every login have to change together, so the podman, frigate, node-red-tm, go2rtc, revproxy, and tm-control tags each update all three.

Tag What it does base Operating system packages, the owner account, and Cockpit. It runs with every -t. full_upgrade The apt full-upgrade, when -u is given wifi The Wi-Fi country, the hotspot (its profile, its password file, the firewall that keeps phones on it from reaching other networks, and the DNS that sends every name on it to the device), and the timer that moves the radio between a saved network and the hotspot. It sets the hotspot's password to the one in the password file, and never restarts a hotspot that is up. go2rtc The camera streaming service on the host, and the stream login Frigate uses to read it detectors Detects the Coral or Hailo accelerator, installs its driver, and writes the boot configuration. See Add an accelerator later. podman The container runtime and the pod frigate Frigate's container, settings, and the devices it needs node-red-tm Node-RED's container, flows, settings, and the radars it needs. Rerun it after plugging in a radar. plate-recognizer The optional Plate Recognizer container revproxy The reverse proxy, with the home page built into its image tm-control The control app and its service, the tm-control command, the record of what was installed that the control app reads, and the setup code while the device isn't claimed. It also updates Frigate's config.yml from earlier versions: the stream login and the settings for the device's login.

docs.title: One run at a time
docs.text: Only one installer run can work on a device at a time. If you start a second run on the device while another is running, it prints "Another install or update is running on this device. Wait for it to finish, then run tmsetup.sh again." and exits before it asks whether to continue or installs anything (with -f, that is after the overwrite question). Runs started with -H don't take part in this: run them one at a time yourself.

docs.title: The device's card
docs.text: When a run on the device ends while the device is unclaimed, the installer shows its card on the terminal: the setup code, and the hotspot's name and password. The card goes only to the terminal, so the hotspot's password stays out of the installer's log; the setup code is still in it. A run from another computer with -H prints a reminder only. sudo tm-control card prints the card on the device at any time.

docs.title: What -f replaces
docs.text:
Every run replaces the container images, service units, Node-RED flows, and the reverse proxy configuration. These files are kept unless you pass -f:

  • /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml
  • /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env
  • /opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/config/config.yml, which holds zones and masks drawn in Frigate
  • /opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/frigate.env. Its Frigate+ key comes from the device's secrets.
  • /opt/traffic-monitor/plate-recognizer/plate-recognizer.env, if Plate Recognizer is installed. Its token and license key come from the device's secrets.

With -f, each is replaced by a fresh copy from its template, and the old file stays next to it with a timestamp in its name so you can copy your settings back. The MQTT broker login carries into the fresh node-red-tm.env and frigate.env. The fresh config.yml has the upload off, so every sharing choice is turned off and none is restored. A fresh Frigate config has detection off and the sample zones, so afterwards turn detection on and redo your zones and masks, as in First-time setup.

The fresh Frigate config keeps one thing from the old one: the model: section, if you chose a model, whether in Frigate's model picker, its configuration editor, or by hand (see Better models). It's kept even when Frigate can't load that model; see If Frigate stops over a model. The installer's own model section for a Coral isn't kept, so the fresh copy gets the model for the accelerator the installer finds. Comments inside a kept section are lost; its keys keep their order. If the old config isn't valid YAML, the fresh copy gets the installer's model section, and the installer says so.

No run, with or without -f, replaces the device's accounts, its setup code, or the passwords and keys in /etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/, including the ThingsBoard token, the Frigate+ API key, and the Plate Recognizer token and license key you entered. The installer writes those values into node-red-tm.env, frigate.env, and plate-recognizer.env on every run, so a fresh copy from -f has them too. The installer takes no secret value as an option: enter the ThingsBoard token on the Sharing page, the Plate Recognizer values on the Device page, and the Frigate+ key on the Detection page.

docs.title: Add an accelerator later
docs.text:
After you add or change a Coral or Hailo accelerator, rerun two tags and reboot when the installer asks:

bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t detectors -t frigate

That installs the driver and gives Frigate's container the device. Frigate's own config.yml still names the old detector, because the installer writes its detectors: and model: sections only when it creates the file. Either edit those two sections by hand to match the template, or add -f to the command above and then redo your Frigate settings, as What -f replaces describes.

-f keeps a model you chose, such as a Frigate+ model, and that model may not suit the new accelerator. If it doesn't, Frigate can't use it and counts nothing, and the Status page reports the problem. Pick a model built for the new accelerator (see Use a model), or, to get the installer's model for it, delete the model: section in Frigate's configuration editor before you run the installer with -f.

docs.title: Reboots
docs.text: The installer edits the boot configuration and installs kernel drivers, so it asks to reboot when needed. On the device, it prompts, and with -y it doesn't ask. Either way the reboot starts one minute later. Remote devices reboot by themselves. Services stay stopped until the reboot.

docs.title: description: The Data export dashboard: download the database or a JSON export, and add comments for whoever analyzes the data.
Data export
docs.text:
Open http://<device>/dashboard/database, or Database in the dashboard's sidebar. This page gets data off the device and lets you leave notes in it. Both downloads need the device's administrator login; a viewer can open the page but not download.

The Data export page

docs.title: Comments
docs.text: A comment is a timestamped note stored in the comments table, for whoever analyzes the data later: a settings change, road work, an event in the area. Give it an effective date and an optional expiry date, the text, and your name; only the name is required. The form also has time fields, but only the dates are kept. Without an effective date, the comment takes effect when you save it. Data and privacy lists the columns.

docs.title: Download the database
docs.text:
Downloads the whole database as a compressed archive named <hostname>_<time>_tmdb.tar.gz. The page shows the database's size in megabytes. The device first makes a consistent copy of the database, so a large one can take a minute or two before the download starts. The copy needs free space about the size of the database; if there isn't enough, the page says so. A 3 GB file can then take about 5 minutes to compress and several more to download. Cancel also works while the copy is being made: the download stops once the copy is done, and no archive is sent. If a download fails, you see the reason instead of a broken file.

On a phone joined to the unit's hotspot, see Phones for how downloads save on Android and on an iPhone.

This download holds the location rounded, as the database stores it. To get a copy with each place's exact location in it, use Download the database with exact locations on the Location page.

Unpack the archive with tar -xvzf on Linux or Mac, or with 7-Zip on Windows. Inside is tmdb.sqlite, which opens in DB Browser for SQLite or any SQLite library.

docs.title: Download JSON
docs.text:
Exports part of the data as JSON files in a compressed archive named <hostname>_<time>_json.tar.gz. Choose what to export and a start and end time, which default to the last 7 days:

Choice Contents Everything The events table, the five radar tables, and the airquality table All event types The whole events table for the time range One object type, such as car or person The events of that type Air quality The airquality table Radar The radar tables

The watch log and the setup history aren't among the exports; they are in the database download.

The files are plain JSON, readable in any text editor or loaded straight into a notebook.

docs.title: description: The Monitoring dashboard: today's counts, car speed statistics, hourly and daily charts, and the latest events with their radar readings.
Monitoring
docs.text:
Open http://<device>/dashboard/monitoring, or open Dashboard from the home page and choose Monitoring in the sidebar. Monitoring shows the counts and speed statistics for one camera and one radar at a time.

The Monitoring page, numbered as in the list below
  1. Sensor selection. A radar and a camera picker, listing every sensor in config.yml, enabled or not. They follow config.yml: each time it changes, each picker keeps its sensor if the file still lists it. Otherwise the camera picker selects the first camera, and the radar picker selects the radar set for the selected camera. When a camera's name in Frigate differs from its entry's name, the camera picker shows Frigate's name in brackets after it. The counts and statistics on this page follow the camera and radar selected on the legacy dashboard at http://<device>/ui/, not the selection here. On a device with one camera and one radar, they're the same.

  2. Car speed statistics for the current day, which starts at 04:00 local time. They cover car events that passed through both zone_capture and zone_radar and got a speed, the radar's or Frigate's. Speeds are absolute values, so inbound and outbound are pooled, and every value is rounded to a whole number.

    The percentiles come from sorting the day's cars by speed and splitting them into 20 groups of equal size, so they're approximate. With few cars, some stay empty: the 25th percentile needs 5 cars, the median 10, the 75th percentile and iqr_upper 15, and the 85th percentile 17.

    Statistic Meaning count Cars with a speed count_radar Cars whose speed came from the radar count_frigate Cars whose speed came from Frigate's estimate, because the radar gave none mean_speed Average speed p25_speed, p50_speed, p75_speed, p85_speed 25th, 50th (median), 75th, and 85th percentile speeds. The 85th percentile is the usual basis for speed limits. max_speed Fastest car count_over_25 Cars faster than 25, in the device's speed unit iqr_upper The outlier line: p75_speed plus 1.5 times the interquartile range iqr_upper_freq Cars faster than iqr_upper, the outliers

  3. Today's counts by object type for events that passed through zone_capture. The day starts at 04:00 local time, so from midnight until 04:00 these counts and the speed statistics are empty. Objects that pass in those hours are left out of the day's counts, but they appear in the hourly and daily charts.

  4. Hourly counts by object type for the last 36 hours, for events that passed through zone_capture.
  5. Daily counts by object type for the last 10 calendar days, for events that passed through zone_capture.
  6. Latest observations. The 21 most recent events from any camera that passed through zone_radar, newest first, including events without a speed. Each card shows Frigate's thumbnail of the object, the direction, the speed, and the radar's raw readings from the start of the event to its end: how many there were ("radar hits"), the range of their magnitudes and speeds, and two charts, Radar Magnitude and Radar Speed. The charts show whether the readings came from one object or from several at once. They're the raw readings, not the ones the speed was worked out from. The list is kept in memory, so it empties when Node-RED restarts.

Counts and statistics come from the events table; see Events. The same counts are published over MQTT on tm/events; see MQTT and ThingsBoard.

docs.title: description: The Movements dashboard: counts of objects by the sequence of zones they passed through, for checking against manual counts.
Movements
docs.text:
Open http://<device>/dashboard/movements. Movements counts objects by the path they took through your zones, which is how you check the device against a manual count or confirm that the zones capture what you want.

Movements come from the entered_zones of each event, so they depend on how the zones are drawn.

The Movements page
  1. Zones. Tick the zones to include. The four standard zone_* zones are unticked by default, so that zones you drew for your own analysis stand out.
  2. Intermediate zones. Choose Show intermediate zones to count each full sequence of zones separately, or Show just initial & final zones to group by where an object entered and where it left.
  3. Time range. Start and end times; the last 7 days by default. In time zones east of UTC, or with a half-hour offset, the page shows no counts for any range.
  4. Counts by object type for each zone sequence that matches.

docs.title: Example: a complex intersection
docs.text:
An intersection with many zones has dozens of possible movements. Each turn or crossing becomes its own row, which you can compare with a manual count sheet.

Twelve zones drawn on a busy five-way intersection Manual confirmation counts; the left sheet matches the zones above

docs.title: Cameras
docs.text:
The control app's Cameras page connects each camera in Frigate to its settings in the Traffic Monitor: whether its events are recorded, which radar gives it speeds, and whether its events go to Plate Recognizer. It also keeps the two in step after you rename or add a camera in Frigate. Only the administrator sees the page.

A camera that was set up by the installer and never renamed works without it. Use the page when you rename a camera in Frigate, add one, pair a camera with a different radar, or want the camera's name kept out of the data the device saves and shares.

docs.title: Two names for each camera
docs.text:
Each camera has two names:

  • Frigate's name is the one in Frigate's configuration, such as oak_ave_wide. Frigate uses it for the camera's streams, zones, and recordings, and for Frigate+. It can say where the camera is: an operator may name a camera after its street. It stays on the device.
  • The name in bold on the Cameras page is the camera's entry in config.yml. It's the name saved with every event and the name the device shares: in the database, in the MQTT messages tm/event and tm/events, in what a server you share data with receives, and in what Plate Recognizer receives.

For a new camera, the page makes the second name for you: camera_ and a number, then six random characters from 0 to 9 and a to f, such as camera_1_3fa9c2. The number tells two cameras apart when you read the page. The random part keeps the name from being used twice on a device, so records from two different cameras never share a name. You can't type one yourself, because a typed name can hold a street again.

A device that has only picam_h265, as the installer sets it up, keeps working with no change: when an entry doesn't say which camera it is, it's the Frigate camera with the same name. picam_h265 doesn't say where the device is, so you can leave it. To switch a camera with a name of your own to a neutral one, see Use a neutral camera name.

docs.title: The Cameras page
docs.text:
Cameras is in the control app's menu, after Detection. At the top, the page says that Frigate owns each camera's name, streams, and zones, and links to Frigate for adding a camera or changing them. Then comes one row for each entry in config.yml, followed by one for each Frigate camera that no entry is paired with. Each row opens, one at a time, to show the camera's settings inside it. A Frigate camera that is turned off there and that no entry is paired with isn't listed: it sends no events. Turn it on in Frigate, and it appears.

An entry's row shows its name in bold, and Frigate's name beside it when the two differ. Under them are its settings and what Frigate has:

  • Frigate detection: whether Frigate detects objects on the camera now. A camera turned off in Frigate detects nothing, so it reads off.
  • Database capture: whether the Traffic Monitor saves the camera's events in its database and sends them on. An event is recorded only when both are on.
  • Radar, and, when the Plate Recognizer add-on is installed, Plates.
  • Recommended zones present and the four zones the flows expect, or Recommended zones missing in Frigate and the ones the camera lacks, or turned off in Frigate and the ones that are there but switched off. Frigate can turn a zone off in its configuration or from its live view, and an object never enters a zone that is off, so it counts as missing for the Traffic Monitor.
  • Other zones enabled: the camera's other zones that are on, by their IDs, with your name beside an ID that Frigate made up. Their IDs are saved with every event; see Zone names are saved with your data.
  • Off in Frigate, when the camera is in Frigate's configuration but turned off there.

An entry whose camera is on in Frigate also has Reference picture on its row, while Frigate answers; see Take a reference picture.

A Frigate camera that no entry is paired with shows its Frigate detection, and Database capture: off.

docs.title: What needs attention
docs.text:
The page marks each problem the Status page's camera checks report, on the camera it's about, in the same colors: red for a problem, amber for a warning. Above the list, a line says how many cameras need attention. Each marked row has a box for each problem that says what's wrong and what to do on this page:

  • Red: a camera is new in Frigate and isn't recorded while Frigate detects objects on it (point an entry at it, or add it), or another entry already records this Frigate camera (remove this one).
  • Amber: Frigate no longer has the camera (point the entry at its new name, or remove it); the camera is turned off in Frigate, Frigate's detection is off, or Database capture is off, so its events aren't recorded; zones are missing or turned off, with a link, Edit its zones in Frigate, that opens Frigate's masks and zones settings at that camera; the camera's radar isn't turned on in config.yml; or a zone's name looks like an address or a person's name.

A grey note names the zones whose names have a word the Traffic Monitor doesn't recognize, and asks you to review them. It isn't a problem, and it doesn't count toward the line above the list.

A row with no box is in step. A new Frigate camera whose Frigate detection is off has no box either: nothing is detected, so nothing is dropped. You can still point an entry at it or add it. The page and the checks come from the same comparison, so they always agree.

When Frigate isn't answering, or has stopped itself in safe mode with no cameras, the page says so and can't compare. The settings stay editable, and the other buttons wait until Frigate answers.

docs.title: Change a camera's settings
docs.text:
Choose Settings on a camera's row. The row opens to its settings. Change them, and choose Save; Cancel closes the row without changing anything.

Setting What it does Frigate detection Frigate's own detection switch for this camera, the same one as in Frigate's live view. It changes when you save, without restarting Frigate, and Frigate keeps it after a restart. Off, Frigate stops detecting objects on the camera, so there are no events to record; it keeps streaming, and recording video if you set it to. Shown only while Frigate answers and the camera is on there. Database capture Off, the Traffic Monitor drops this camera's events: nothing is saved in the database or sent on. Frigate keeps detecting either way. Radar The radar that supplies this camera's speeds. Direction comes from the zones' order on any camera, and from the radar only when the zones give none. No radar records the camera's events with the zones' direction, and with a speed only from Frigate, where you've set up a speed zone. One radar can serve several cameras. Send plates to Plate Recognizer Shown only when the add-on is installed. See Plate Recognizer.

The drop-down lists the radars the device was installed with, each with its state:

  • off in config.yml: the radar's entry has enabled: false, so it reads nothing.
  • port closed: Node-RED hasn't opened the radar's serial port, for example because the radar was plugged in after the install. A radar that is off in config.yml shows both marks. See First-time setup.
  • not set up in config.yml: the radar has no entry under sensors.radars, so it can't be chosen. Pairing a camera with it would record no speeds.
  • missing: the camera's current radar isn't one of the device's radars. Choose another, or No radar.

Radar settings themselves, such as turning a radar off, stay in config.yml. Which way a sensor faces is set on the Location page.

docs.title: After renaming a camera in Frigate
docs.text:
When you rename a camera in Frigate, the Traffic Monitor doesn't know the new name belongs to the same camera, and records nothing from it until you say so.

  1. In Frigate's configuration editor, rename the camera and choose Save & Restart. Frigate uses the new name only after it restarts, so Save alone changes nothing yet.
  2. Open the Cameras page. The old entry reads Frigate no longer has the old name, and the new name has its own row, new in Frigate and isn't recorded. If Frigate's detection is off for the camera, the new row has no box, because nothing is being dropped, but it still offers Point. If the old entry's Database capture is off too, it has no box either, because nothing was being recorded from it, and the new row still offers Point.
  3. On the new row, choose Point <entry> at this, and confirm.

The entry keeps its name and settings, so the camera's records carry on under the same name, in the same deployment, with nothing changed in the database. If two cameras were renamed together, each new row offers a button for each entry whose camera is gone. To choose the right pair, look at the entries' rows: each shows Frigate's old name for its camera and its radar. An entry whose camera is only turned Off in Frigate isn't offered, because that camera still exists.

Until you point the entry at the new name, the Status page's Cameras in config.yml check is a problem. While Frigate's detection is off for the camera, it's a warning instead, about the old entry, whose camera is gone. If the entry's Database capture is off as well, the check passes, because nothing is being dropped. Pointing the entry at the new name doesn't turn Database capture on; do that in its settings if you want the camera recorded.

docs.title: Add a camera
docs.text: A Frigate camera that no entry is paired with isn't recorded. On its row, choose Add as new. The row opens to the new entry's settings, with Database capture on, No radar, and plates off. Choose the radar, and Add. The page gives the entry its name.

docs.title: Use a neutral camera name
docs.text:
An entry whose name isn't of the form camera_<number>_<six characters> has Use a neutral camera name on its row. Choose it to switch the camera to a name the page makes, such as camera_2_81d0e4. The entry keeps its settings and its place in config.yml, and remembers the old name as Frigate's name, so the pairing doesn't change.

Records already saved keep the old name. They can't be renamed here, because rewriting a database of several gigabytes on a microSD card takes a long time. The dashboards' charts start again under the new name, and Node-RED ends the camera's deployment under the old name and starts one under the new one, at the same place and facing the same way. The confirmation says so before it does anything. A server that receives the device's data sees the old sensor end and a new one start.

docs.title: Remove an entry
docs.text: An entry whose Frigate camera is gone, because you deleted the camera or renamed it and pointed no entry at the new name, has Remove. Choose it and confirm. The entry's settings are removed from config.yml, and Node-RED ends the camera's deployment. Records already saved are kept. The same button removes an entry that repeats another entry's Frigate camera.

docs.title: Take a reference picture
docs.text:
Reference picture gives you one zip for a tool that places recorded paths on a street: a still picture of what the camera sees, the same view with its zones marked, and the zones' shapes and sizes. Both pictures are the size of Frigate's detect frame, so paths and boxes recorded as fractions of that frame line up with them.

File What it holds <name>_clean.jpg The camera's current frame from Frigate, with nothing drawn on it <name>_zones.jpg The same view a moment later, drawn by Frigate with the outline of each zone that is on, in the zone's colour <name>.json The data file: the place, the camera, how it is mounted, when the pictures were taken, and every zone; see The data file <name>_zones.svg A drawing made by the control app: the clean picture with each zone outlined and named, and a legend below it

The four files share one name, such as tm-reference_3f9a1c2e-si_camera_1_3fa9c2_20261118T183005Z: the ID of the place in use (no-place when there is none), the camera's name (the one in bold on its row), and when the clean picture was taken, in UTC.

  1. On the camera's row, choose Reference picture. The dialog says what the picture gives away before any picture is taken.
  2. Wait until nobody is in view, and choose Take the pictures. The dialog shows both pictures and the camera's zones with their colours and side lengths.
  3. Look at both pictures. The device doesn't check them for people, so this is up to you. If anyone is in them, wait, and choose Take again.
  4. Leave Include this place's exact location ticked to put the place's location in the data file, or clear it.
  5. Choose Save the zip.

On a phone joined to the unit's hotspot, the pictures show in Android's sign-in window but the zip doesn't save there, the same as Download diagnostics. Like it, the zip saves from a browser, on a computer or on the phone after the steps under Phones.

docs.title: What the picture gives away
docs.text:
The dialog opens with this note:

This picture shows your street. Anyone who has it can tell where the unit is, and it shows whoever was in view. The device doesn't check the pictures for people. You are responsible for making sure nobody is in either picture before you save them: look at both, and if anyone is in them, wait and take them again. Share them only with people you would give the unit's exact location. The data file also holds that location unless you clear the box below.

  • The location in the data file is the place's exact location, as set on the Location page, not the rounded one the database keeps. When the place in use has no location, the box is greyed and the data file holds none.
  • The device holds the pictures in memory for 10 minutes, for the administrator who took them, and never saves them. Closing the dialog, taking them again, or restarting the control app drops them sooner. They're never in the database, the exports, the diagnostics file, or anything the device uploads.
  • The audit log records each picture taken and each zip saved, with the camera's name and whether the location was included, never the location itself.

docs.title: When it can't take the pictures
docs.text:
• This camera is turned off in Frigate. Turn it on in Frigate first.
  • Frigate has no live picture from this camera right now. The camera isn't sending, or Frigate has only an older frame. Check the camera on the Status page, then try again.
  • These pictures are no longer held on the device. Ten minutes have passed, you took another picture, or the control app restarted. Take them again.

docs.title: The two drawings
docs.text: The zones picture is Frigate's own drawing: outlines only, of the zones that are on, with no names. The SVG is the control app's, drawn on the clean picture from the data file. It outlines each zone that is on in its colour and names it, and letters the corners of each zone with side lengths (or, when no zone has any, of each zone with four corners). Its legend lists every zone, with its side lengths, or off in Frigate, not drawn, or no outline for a zone with fewer than three corners.

docs.title: The data file
docs.text:
Field What it holds format, format_version traffic-monitor-reference and 1 survey_id The ID of the place in use, or null camera The camera's name (the one in bold on its row) deployment_id The camera's open deployment at the place, or null location {"lat": …, "lon": …}, the place's exact location, or null when the box was cleared or there was no location to include pose How the camera is mounted, as the control app records it for the camera when the picture is taken (see the Pose field table below), or null when nothing is recorded for the camera or its entry is turned off in config.yml pictures Each file's name, and for the two pictures taken_at, in UTC, such as 2026-11-18T18:30:05Z traffic_monitor_version, frigate_version The versions running when the pictures were taken detect The width and height of Frigate's detect frame in pixels, which is the pictures' size distance_unit The unit of the zones' side lengths: ft when Frigate's interface is set to imperial units, else m zones Every zone of the camera, in Frigate's order, with the fields in the Zone field table below Pose field What it holds heading_deg The way the camera faces, in degrees clockwise from true north (0 to 359), or null pitch_deg How far below level the camera is tilted, in degrees (0 to 90), or null height_m The camera's height above the road, in metres, or null view_distance_m The distance along the ground from the camera to the centre of its view, in metres, or null mount The usual mount the recording started from, such as pole, or null hfov_deg Always null for now. It is kept for the camera's horizontal field of view

The pose is for placing the recorded paths on a street plan. It holds no coordinate, name, or description, so it goes into the data file whether or not the box for the place's exact location is ticked. The drawing's caption says which way the camera faces, such as facing NE (40°), when a heading is recorded.

Zone field What it holds key The zone's ID color The colour Frigate draws the zone in, as #rrggbb, or null enabled Whether the zone is on in Frigate drawn Whether the zone is outlined in the pictures: it's on and has at least three corners corners Each corner's letter (A, B, C, and on, in the order Frigate stores the corners) and its x and y as fractions of the frame's width and height, from the top-left corner, even where Frigate's configuration holds the zone in pixels. A corner past the frame's edge is below 0 or above 1 distances The side lengths entered in Frigate for speed estimation, in Frigate's order, or [] sides The same lengths by side, in the order Frigate stores the corners, such as {"start": "A", "end": "B", "length": 12}; the last side ends at A. [] unless there is one length for each corner inertia, loitering_time, speed_threshold, objects The zone's settings in Frigate filters For each object with filters in the zone, the ones that are numbers among min_area, max_area, min_ratio, max_ratio, threshold, and min_score. Any other filter is left out

The names you typed for zones in Frigate's editor and the place's description are never in the data file or the drawing. Frigate's name for the camera isn't either, unless the camera's entry uses it as its own name, as the installer's picam_h265 does: then it's in the files' names, the data file, and the drawing. To keep it out, use a neutral camera name first.

docs.title: Zone names are saved with your data
docs.text:
A zone's ID is saved with every event that enters it: in the database, in the exports, and in what the device uploads. Frigate makes the ID from the name you type in its zone editor, in lower case with _ for spaces, so 1420 Oak St is saved as 1420_oak_st. Name zones for what they are, such as a compass direction (zone_north) or a lane (zone_lane_bus), not for a street, a house number, or a person.

A name with other punctuation, or with letters outside a to z, gets an ID that Frigate makes up, such as zone_a9bacc03. The page shows your name beside that ID and doesn't check it, because the ID says nothing about the place.

The page checks the IDs of each camera's other zones that are on:

  • On a camera whose events are recorded, an amber box names the zones whose names look like an address or a person's name: a number of three or more digits, an apostrophe, a street abbreviation such as st or ave, or a street word such as lane or strasse together with an ordinal such as 5th or a word the check doesn't recognize. The Status page's Zone names check warns too.
  • A grey note names the zones whose names have a word the check doesn't recognize. The check knows about 200 English words for parts of a road, directions, and what moves on it, and can't tell whether another word is a street's name or a person's. A word in another language written in a to z, such as nord, gets the note too, so review the names and leave them if they're fine.

To rename a zone, choose Edit its zones in Frigate and change its name there. Its ID follows the new name.
