While the zone is on one of the camera's required-zones lists in Frigate (for reviews, snapshots, MQTT, and a few others), or a Frigate profile changes it, Frigate keeps its ID and changes only its name, and the page goes on showing the old ID: take the zone off those lists, rename it, then add it back under its new ID. Events already saved keep the old ID. The page never changes a zone itself.

docs.title: What still carries Frigate's name
docs.text:
The Traffic Monitor keeps Frigate's name out of what it saves and shares. These places still carry the name:

  • Frigate's own database, and its recordings and snapshots. Frigate keeps events under its own camera names.
  • Frigate's frigate/events messages on the device's MQTT broker. Anything subscribed to the broker sees them. Frigate publishes them, not the Traffic Monitor.
  • Frigate+. The name identifies the camera for the scene conditions and annotations you submit.
  • A reference picture of an entry named for its Frigate camera. The files' names, the data file, and the drawing carry the entry's name, which is then Frigate's name too. See Take a reference picture.
  • Records saved before a switch. A device whose entry was named by hand has saved that name with its records, and keeps it there after you use a neutral camera name.

The Status page shows Frigate's camera names to anyone who is logged in, as Frigate does. The diagnostics file replaces them before you send it to someone; that section lists its limits.

To change the entries by hand, see sensors.cameras.

docs.title: Control app and login
docs.text:
The device's home page is its control app. It holds the device's accounts, and one login there opens the apps your account may use: the dashboards, Frigate, the Node-RED editor, and the camera feeds. Cockpit has its own address and its own login. Its Status, Device, and Date and time pages show whether the device works and help you fix it; see Check and fix the device. Its Detection page shows the object detection model and lets the administrator change it; see Choose the detection model. Its Cameras page keeps each camera's settings in step with Frigate; see Cameras. Its Location page records where the device is and how precisely the database stores it; see Places and location. Its Sharing page chooses whether the device uploads its data to a server and how much of its location goes with it; see Share data. Its About page names the open source projects the device is built on and gives the license notices. These accounts belong to the device. They're separate from the Raspberry Pi user account you created when you imaged the card. That account's password is the system password.

What the login protects

The login keeps people on your network out of the apps. The device uses plain HTTP, so passwords and images cross your network unencrypted. Use the device on a network you trust.

docs.title: Claim the device
docs.text:
A device that has no administrator yet sends every page to setup. That happens on a new device, after an update from a version without the login, and after reset-admin. Setup has five steps: a welcome page, the license agreement, the administrator account, the system password, and sharing.

You need the setup code, eight letters and digits written as XXXX-XXXX. It comes from one of two places:

  • A pre-built unit: the card that came with the device.

  • A device you installed yourself: the end of the installer's output, in a line like this one:

    This device isn't claimed yet. Open http://tm-01.local/ (or its IP address) and enter the setup code ABCD-EFGH
to create the administrator account. The code works once.

    The installer prints the same code on every run until the device is claimed. The installer's log, ~/tmsetup-<date>-<time>.log on the computer that ran it, has the same output. On the device, sudo tm-control card shows the code with the device's hotspot name and password, and sudo cat /etc/traffic-monitor/setup-code shows the code alone.

To claim the device:

  1. Open http://<device>/. Home page and apps explains how to find the address. On the device's own hotspot, the phone's sign-in window opens it for you; see Wi-Fi and the hotspot.
  2. Choose Start setup, read the license agreement, and accept it.
  3. Enter the setup code, then a username and password for the administrator account. Usernames are 3 to 32 characters: lowercase letters, digits, dots, dashes, and underscores. Passwords are at least 10 characters.
  4. Choose Claim this device. You're logged in as the administrator.
  5. Set a new system password, or choose Skip for now.
  6. Choose Not now, or, on a device that already has a ThingsBoard access token, set up sharing. Nothing is shared unless you turn it on, and the Sharing page is there later.
Step 3 of setup creates the administrator account

The code works once. After several wrong codes, setup makes you wait before the next try, a little longer after each wrong code.

When the license agreement changes

An update can bring a new version of the license agreement. Until the administrator accepts it, nobody can open the apps. The administrator sees the new version after logging in. Viewers see Waiting for an administrator until it's accepted.

docs.title: The system password
docs.text:
The system password is the password of the Raspberry Pi user account: the one you log in to Cockpit and SSH with. Setup offers to change it, with a Use the same password as my account checkbox. Skip the step to keep the password the account has. To change it later, use Cockpit's Accounts page, or run passwd over SSH.

If someone else installed the device, you may not know the account's name. Setup's system-password step and the home page's Cockpit tile show it to the administrator.

docs.title: Log in
docs.text:
Open the home page or any app. Without a session, the device shows its login page, then takes you to the page you asked for. You stay logged in for a week, and using the device keeps the session going. To log out, choose Log out in the menu. Frigate's own Logout also logs you out of the device.

After five wrong passwords in a row, the device makes you wait before the next try: a few seconds at first, and twice as long after each further wrong password, up to 5 minutes. It counts wrong passwords for the account and for the address they come from, so a wait for an account applies on every phone and computer. Sessions that are already logged in keep working. The count clears 15 minutes after the last wrong password, or when the login succeeds.

docs.title: Administrators and viewers
docs.text:
Each device has one administrator, the account created when it was claimed, and any number of viewers.

App or page Administrator Viewer Dashboard and Legacy Dashboard Yes Yes Downloads on the Data export page Yes No Frigate: live view, review, and explore Yes Yes Frigate: settings and the configuration editor Yes No Node-RED editor and Camera feeds Yes No The Users page Yes No Status, Device, and Date and time pages Yes Read only; see What viewers see The Detection page Yes Read only; see The Detection page The Cameras page Yes No The Location page Yes No The Sharing page Yes Read only; see What viewers see The About page Yes Yes

A viewer who opens an administrator's app from a link sees a page that says so, with a way back to the home page.

Cockpit uses the Raspberry Pi user account, not these accounts.

docs.title: Add a viewer
docs.text:
1. Open Users from the menu.
  2. Under Add a viewer, enter a username and a password, and choose Add viewer.
  3. Give the person the username and password.

Each viewer's menu on the Users page has Set a new password, which also logs them out everywhere, and Remove.

docs.title: Change your password
docs.text:
Open Account from the menu. Under Change your password, enter your current password and the new one. Every other browser and phone where you were logged in is logged out; this one stays logged in. Wrong current passwords count toward the same wait as wrong logins.

Log out everywhere, on the same page, ends your sessions in every browser and on every phone, including the one you're using. Use it if you logged in on a device that isn't yours.

docs.title: If you forget a password
docs.text:
• A viewer's password: the administrator sets a new one on the Users page.
  • The administrator's password: see the next section.

docs.title: If the administrator's password is lost
docs.text:
Someone who can log in to the device with the Raspberry Pi user account can start over. Open a terminal over SSH, or in Cockpit at http://<device>:9090, and run:

sudo tm-control reset-admin

It removes every account, the administrator and all viewers, and prints a new setup code. Then claim the device again with that code. Your data and settings stay as they are.

docs.title: If the control app is down
docs.text:
When the control app doesn't answer, the apps can't check your login. Every app then shows a page that says the control app isn't answering, and the home page says The control app isn't answering. To start it again:

  • In a browser, open Cockpit at http://<device>:9090. It doesn't need the control app. Log in with your Raspberry Pi user account, go to Services, open tm-control.service, and restart it.

  • Over SSH, run:

    sudo systemctl restart tm-control.service
sudo journalctl -u tm-control.service -n 50   # if it stops again, the reason is in its log

An app that's down while the control app works, such as Frigate during a restart, shows a 502 Bad Gateway error instead. System administration covers the services and their logs.

docs.title: Choose the detection model
docs.text: The control app's Detection page shows what the device looks for and which AI model does the looking, and lets the administrator change the model without SSH. Frigate runs the model on the device's detector: a Coral or Hailo accelerator, or the processor when there's none. To get a better model for a difficult site, see Better models.

docs.title: The Detection page
docs.text:
Detection is in the control app's menu, after Device. The page opens with a line on what it's for, then four sections:

  • Object detection gives the Detector, such as edgetpu for a Coral, and the Running model. It also tells you when Frigate isn't answering.
  • Model in use is the model Frigate runs, as one card. The card holds everything about the running model, including the objects it recognises and the objects the device tracks. The card is always there once the page has loaded the models, even when Frigate isn't answering or doesn't name its model. The section is left out only when the page can't load the models.
  • Frigate+ is how to get a Frigate+ model, and where administrators set the API key and use a model by its ID.
  • Other models on this device lists the rest, and its title counts them.

Each model is a card with its name, its kind (Frigate+ or local), and when it was trained and what it's built for (when it says). Select Files and objects on a card to see its files, with their sizes and the start of each file's SHA-256 hash, and the objects it recognises. A model with no list of objects has Files instead, and the running model's card with no files has Objects. A mark says when the model is:

Mark Meaning In use Frigate runs this model. can't run on this detector The model is built for another detector than the device's, so Use is off. incomplete The model has its file but not its .json, or the other way round.

The model the installer set up is shown as The installer's model. It has no .json, and it can't be deleted. A device without a Coral has no installer's model: Frigate then runs its own built-in model until you choose another, and the page shows it as Frigate's built-in model, which can't be deleted either.

Everyone who can log in sees the models, the object lists, and the Frigate+ text. Administrators also get Upload a model, under the Other models on this device heading, then Use, Download, and Delete on each model, the Frigate+ API key, and Use a model by its ID. While Frigate runs another model, the device's default (the installer's model, or Frigate's built-in model on a device without a Coral) has a Use of its own.

When Frigate isn't answering, the page says so and shows what Frigate's config file says. The same when Frigate started in safe mode because it couldn't use its config: the page says so, nothing is detected meanwhile, and Use on a model, or on the installer's model, gives Frigate a config it can run. In both cases the model in use still has its card, made from the config file. The objects Frigate tracks aren't known while it's down, so that list is empty, and the recognised list is there only when the model has a .json or the installer's labels file. A model that Frigate runs but the device has no entry for gets a card too, named for the model or Unknown model.

docs.title: Upload a model
docs.text:
A model is a model file and a small .json file beside it, its sidecar, which tells Frigate how to use it. Choose Upload a model under Other models on this device, then pick one of these:

  • A package from whoever trained the model: a zip or tar.gz with the model file and its .json at the top level, not inside a folder. A zip must be stored or deflate-compressed, which is what ordinary zip tools make. If the package has a SHA256SUMS file, the device checks the files against it.
  • The two files, the model file and its .json. The .json must be named for the model file: mine.tflite and mine.tflite.json. The page sends the .json first.
  • A model file alone. The page then asks for what Frigate needs to know about it and writes the .json for you. The settings are a name for the model list (the file name when left empty), the model type, the width and height of its input, the input tensor, the pixel format, optionally the input data type, and the labels, one per line in the model's order. On a device with a Coral or Hailo accelerator, the fields start with Frigate's example for that detector. The values come from the model's documentation; Frigate's reference config lists what each setting accepts.
  • A .json alone, to finish a model file that's on the device already.

The page shows every file when you pick, because a Frigate+ model's file has no extension.

The limits are 100 MB for a model file, 2 MB for a .json, and at least 512 MB of free storage left afterwards. A model whose name is already on the device is refused; delete the old one first. A model file can't be named default, which the page keeps for the device's default. A model has to be built for the device's detector. The page marks one that isn't, and won't use it.

Take models only from a source you trust

A model is code that the detector runs. A model from an unknown source can make the device count wrongly or fail. Upload only models you trained, or that come from a source you trust.

docs.title: Use a model
docs.text:
Choose Use on a model and confirm. Frigate checks the whole configuration with the model in it and saves it, and then the device restarts Frigate. A restart takes about a minute, and the device counts nothing meanwhile. The page asks every few seconds and says when Frigate runs the model. If Frigate hasn't come back after 90 seconds, the page says so and links to the Status page.

If Frigate refuses the change, the page shows Frigate's reason, and nothing changes. When Frigate isn't answering at all, the device edits Frigate's config.yml itself, keeps a backup beside it, and restarts Frigate. That's how Use on The installer's model gets a device out of a bad choice without SSH. On a device without a Coral, Use on Frigate's built-in model does the same.

The page refuses a Use in these cases:

  • Frigate is restarting. Try again in a minute.
  • Frigate is downloading a model by its ID, or the device is applying another model change. Wait for it to finish.
  • The device's detector can't be told, because Frigate isn't answering and its config file can't be read, so the model can't be checked against it.
  • Frigate's config sets a model inside a detector, which would override this one. Remove that model in Frigate's config editor first.
  • The installer's model file is gone from the device.

docs.title: Download a model
docs.text:
Download saves a zip with the model's file, its .json, and a SHA256SUMS file. The files are byte for byte what's on the device, so the zip is a backup, or a way to put the same model on another device with Upload a model. A .json keeps every field it came with, including ones the page doesn't show.

A model without a .json the device can read downloads as its model file alone, under the file's own name, and the page says so before it starts. Whoever uploads that file is asked for what Frigate needs to know about it. The installer's model and Frigate's built-in model download this way too. A device keeps their file names for its own copies, so rename such a file before you upload it.

docs.title: Delete a model
docs.text: Delete asks first, then removes both of the model's files. It can't remove the model Frigate runs, the installer's model, or Frigate's built-in model. To delete the model that's running, use another model first, such as The installer's model.

docs.title: What the model recognises
docs.text:
The model in use's card holds two lists of objects. Select Files and objects on it to see them, above the model's files. The card first says that Frigate tracks only the objects in both lists, then gives:

  • Objects the running model recognises is what the running model can detect. The line under its title says where the list came from: Frigate when it answers, otherwise the model's .json or the installer's labels file. Objects the device also tracks are filled. Frigate fills the gaps in a model's label map with entries named unknown, which the page leaves out, so its count can be lower than the label map's.
  • Objects tracked on this device is the objects Frigate is set to track, from its objects: track lists. Objects the running model doesn't recognise are amber, and the title counts them.

Each list with objects in it has a Copy button, and both lists are shown whenever Files and objects is open.

To track more of what the model recognises, change the lists in Frigate's configuration editor; see Tune object detection. An object that's tracked but not recognised is also named on the card itself, under Tracked but not recognised by the running model, so you see it while Files and objects is closed. The model can't detect it, so the device never counts it.

The other models' cards each have their own Objects it recognises list, read from that model's .json or, for the installer's model, its labels file. Frigate's built-in model has none. On those cards, a line names the tracked objects that model doesn't recognise, which the device would stop counting if you switched to it.

The recognised list comes from Frigate, and the model's .json has a list of its own. They should agree. When Frigate's list has different objects, a line above the lists says "Frigate reports a different list than this model's .json." This is rare, and it usually means someone edited the label map in Frigate's config on purpose.

docs.title: Frigate+
docs.text:
Frigate+ trains models on snapshots from your device. There are three ways to get one onto it:

  • By its ID: when the device has internet and a Frigate+ API key, an administrator pastes the model's ID on this page, and Frigate downloads the model.
  • In Frigate: pick the model in Frigate, under Settings > System > Detectors and model, and Frigate downloads it. Then choose Use here if Frigate doesn't run it already.
  • Offline: upload the model's two files on this page, as a package from whoever trained the model, or copied from another device's Frigate. See A device without internet.

The text shows for everyone, and the section is there even when the page can't load the models. Administrators get two panels under it, above Other models on this device. Both are closed until you select their titles. A viewer sees the text and no panels.

docs.title: The API key
docs.text:
The panel titled API key holds the key. The Status page's Set the key opens it. The key is kept with the device's other secrets, not in config.yml.

  • The page never shows the key back. Beside the panel's title is a short note on whether the key is set: "not set", "set", or "set, ending in" its last four characters for a key of 12 or more characters. A set key's note adds ", in use" while Frigate runs a Frigate+ model; "not set" never does.
  • Save stores what you typed. A key is 36 characters, a colon, and 40 lowercase letters or digits, as Frigate+ shows it; the page refuses anything else. The eye icon shows the key while you type.
  • Remove asks first, then empties the key. Without a key, snapshots can't be submitted to Frigate+. A Frigate+ model whose files are on the device keeps running; one that isn't downloaded yet stops Frigate until the key is set again, and the Status page's Frigate+ check says so.
  • Saving or removing restarts Frigate, which takes about a minute. The device counts nothing meanwhile.

The ThingsBoard token is on the Sharing page, and the Plate Recognizer keys are on the Device page.

docs.title: Use a model by its ID
docs.text:
The panel titled Use a model by its ID is for a model you've trained and have as an ID on the Frigate+ website. To download a model, the device needs the API key above, internet, and a Frigate that answers.

  1. On the Frigate+ website, open your models and copy the model's ID: 32 characters, each 0-9 or a-f. An address that starts with plus:// works too, and so does an ID with spaces around it. The page refuses anything else before it sends anything.
  2. Paste it into Model ID and choose Download and use, then confirm.
  3. Frigate downloads the model while it checks the configuration with the model in it. This can take a few minutes, and the device waits up to 10 minutes. The panel says that Frigate is downloading, and Use, Upload a model, Download, and Delete are off meanwhile. You can leave the page: the device keeps following the download, and when you open the page again it shows the download while it runs, or why it failed.
  4. When Frigate has saved the configuration, the device restarts Frigate, which takes about a minute. The page then says when Frigate runs the model, as it does after Use. Traffic isn't counted while Frigate restarts.

If the device already has the model's two files, there's nothing to download: the box does what Use on the model's card does, and the confirmation is Use's too: it names the model and the button reads Use.

A download ends in one of these ways:

What the panel says What happened Frigate runs the model. Frigate downloaded the model, saved the configuration, and restarted. Frigate refused the model, with Frigate's reason. Frigate checked the configuration and said no, for example because the key is wrong or Frigate+ doesn't know the ID. Frigate's config is unchanged. Frigate didn't finish downloading the model in 10 minutes. The device stopped waiting. The download may have been slow, or Frigate may have refused the model too late for the device to hear. Check the device's internet connection, then try again. Frigate stopped before the download finished. Frigate restarted or went down, for example after a key change or a restart from the Status page, so the download was lost. Try again once Frigate runs. Frigate answered with a number, or the download couldn't be followed. Rare. Frigate answered the save with something unexpected, or the device couldn't keep following the download because of an error of its own. Try again, and if it repeats, download the diagnostics from the Device page.

The device refuses to start a download when no key is set, when Frigate isn't answering (unlike Use, it doesn't edit Frigate's config file itself), or while another model change is going on.

A model built for another detector than the device's is downloaded, and Frigate then refuses it. Its files stay on the device, and it's listed under Other models on this device as unable to run here. A model whose download went wrong may stay on the device in a state Frigate won't load. Choose Delete on its card, then enter the ID again.

docs.title: Check and fix the device
docs.text:
Four pages in the control app's menu tell you whether the device works and let the administrator fix the common problems from a phone, without SSH. A fifth, Detection, shows the object detection model and changes it:

  • Status checks the services, apps, settings, hardware, network, and clock, and offers a fix for what's wrong.
  • Device shows the device's facts and software versions, and has the diagnostics download, reboot, and shut down.
  • Date and time compares the device's clock with your phone's or computer's and sets it.
  • Network shows the device's names and addresses, and lets the administrator change the hotspot. See The Network page.

The home page shows the Status page's summary under the device's name, such as Everything is working. Tap it to open the Status page.

docs.title: The Status page
docs.text:
The page opens with one sentence about the whole device:

Summary Meaning Everything is working Every check passed. Working, with 2 things to look at Some checks have a warning, and none has a problem. 2 problems need attention At least one check has a problem. Some checks couldn't run Some checks couldn't get an answer, and none found a warning or a problem.

Below it, each check shows a mark, its name, and one or two sentences about what it found and what to do. A tick means it passed, a triangle a warning, a cross a problem, and a question mark that the check couldn't run. The page checks again every 10 seconds while it's open. Refresh checks at once.

The checks come in groups:

Group What it checks Services Each Traffic Monitor service: running, stopped, starting, or running after restarts that followed failures. Frigate restarts itself when you save its config; that doesn't count as a failure. When it restarts itself again and again within minutes, as when its AI accelerator has failed, that does count, and the row says so. Apps Frigate answers, isn't in safe mode (with no cameras because of a config error), and gets frames from each camera. When Frigate stopped on an error, the Frigate check quotes it. When Frigate isn't answering because it keeps stopping itself, the check says so and points at the Hardware group and the diagnostics. Node-RED answers, loaded config.yml without errors, and has its database at the version this install expects. The camera streams run, and Frigate reads them. The MQTT broker requires its login while port 1883 is open to the network. The Sharing server check says how the server the device uploads to last answered; see Check that the server gets the data. The Setup history check says whether the device is recording the detection model and camera settings; see The setup history checks. Configuration Frigate and config.yml agree on the names that link them: each Frigate camera has an entry under sensors.cameras that is enabled (see The camera checks), it has the zones zone_capture, zone_near, zone_far, and zone_radar, no other zone has a name that looks like an address or a person's name, each radar under sensors.radars is named after one of the TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_ variables in node-red-tm.env, and each camera's radar is enabled. The Location check is a problem when a deployment value in config.yml is one Node-RED won't accept, such as a coordinate out of range or a heading that isn't a whole number from 0 to 359, and names the key. It warns when a sensor still has its own lat or lon, when a bearing, the old name for which way a sensor faces, is still in the file (Node-RED converts one of the eight compass points when it next starts, and any other value is yours to replace with heading_deg, as If your file still says bearing explains), when the device's places haven't been set up since an update, which the control app does by itself once Node-RED answers, and when survey_id names a place the device doesn't have, and links to the Location page. In safe mode Frigate has no cameras, so the checks that read them, here and in the Apps group, report that they couldn't run and point at the Frigate check. It also checks the ThingsBoard upload: its settings, and that a token is set when the upload is on. The Sharing check says what the device shares and warns when the Sharing page needs a look. The Frigate+ check says whether a Frigate+ key and a Frigate+ model are set together, and whether Frigate can use the model; see The Frigate+ check. The Model and profile names check warns when the running model's title, a local model's file name, or Frigate's active profile has a name that looks like an address or a person's name, because all three are saved in the database; see The setup history checks. See config.yml settings and First-time setup. Hardware Each AI accelerator, from plugged in to passed to Frigate and listed in its config, or a warning when there's none and Frigate detects on the CPU. Whether detection works is Frigate's to report: when its detector keeps failing, Frigate restarts itself, and the Services and Apps rows say so. The video decoder Frigate uses for the camera. Each radar, from plugged in to read by Node-RED. Network The device's Wi-Fi, in four checks. An offline device is normal, so none of them is a problem for lack of internet. See The Network group. Device Free storage (a warning under 2 GB, a problem under 512 MB), free memory (a warning under 200 MB), the processor's temperature (a warning from 80 °C, a problem from 85 °C), and the power supply: whether the Pi ran short of power or slowed itself down since it started. Date and time Whether the clock was ever set, and whether it keeps time from the internet.

docs.title: The Network group
docs.text:
Check What it says Hotspot On as TM-4F2A, at http://10.42.0.1/ while the hotspot is up. Standing by while the device is on a saved network; the hotspot starts when that network is out of reach. Off by choice when the hotspot is turned off. A problem when the hotspot isn't set up (rerun the installer with -t wifi), the Wi-Fi radio is switched off, the hotspot should be on and isn't (Restart the hotspot), the hotspot has no password (Set a password opens the Network page; see also A hotspot you set up by hand), a USB Wi-Fi adapter has taken the built-in radio's place, or the hotspot's firewall isn't loaded. A warning when the hotspot isn't secured with WPA2. Wi-Fi network The network the device is on and its signal, or that it has no saved network, or that none of the saved networks is in reach. The Network page lists the saved networks and lets an administrator join a network, reorder them, and forget them. Internet Reachable, or Not reachable. That's normal for an offline unit. It also says when the network needs a sign-in page, so the device has no internet. It is never a warning or a problem. Wi-Fi country The country, or a warning that none is set. Rerun the installer with -t wifi and it asks; see The Wi-Fi country.

A check that can't read the Wi-Fi state shows a question mark.

docs.title: Fix a problem
docs.text:
A check that isn't passing offers one of these:

  • A Restart button, such as Restart Frigate, for a service that stopped or keeps failing. The Hotspot check's Restart the hotspot has the device look at its Wi-Fi radio and start the hotspot if it should be on. The device asks first and says what you'll notice, for example that traffic isn't counted while Frigate restarts. A note under the button says when the restart is under way.
  • Re-scan hardware, at the end of the Hardware group while one of its checks isn't passing. It runs every check again at once, so you don't wait for the next check after you plug a device back in or follow the check's advice.
  • A link to the page that fixes it, such as Set the date and time, Diagnostics on the Device page, or Set the token or Check the token for the ThingsBoard upload, which open the token's section of the Sharing page, or Review sharing, which opens the same page, or Set the key and Choose a model for Frigate+, which open the API key panel and the Use a model by its ID panel in the Frigate+ section of the Detection page, or Open the Location page for the Location check, or Open the Cameras page (see Cameras) for the camera, zone, and radar-pairing checks.
  • A sentence with the next step, such as rerunning the installer for Node-RED (tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm; see Installer options).

docs.title: The camera checks
docs.text:
The Cameras in config.yml check compares Frigate's cameras with the entries under sensors.cameras in config.yml. An entry points at the Frigate camera named by its frigate_camera setting, or, when it has none, at the camera with the same name as the entry. The control app's Cameras page keeps the two in step; each problem below links to it, and the page marks the camera each one is about.

Result Meaning Problem A camera that is on in Frigate, with Frigate's detection on, has no entry pointing at it, so its events aren't recorded. Or two entries point at the same Frigate camera, and only the first is used. Warning An entry is enabled, but Frigate doesn't have that camera, or has it turned off. Or a camera's events are dropped on one side: its Database capture is off while Frigate detects objects on it, or Frigate's detection is off while its Database capture is on. Either is fine if you turned it off on purpose. Passed Every camera that is on in Frigate has an entry, and each one's Frigate detection and Database capture are both on, so its events are recorded, or both off, so nothing is detected and nothing is dropped. A camera with no entry passes when its Frigate detection is off. Couldn't run Frigate isn't answering or is in safe mode, so it has no cameras to compare, or config.yml can't be read.

The check names an entry by its name in config.yml and, when that differs, Frigate's name for the camera in brackets. The Zones check looks at the same pairs: it warns when a camera that is on in Frigate and enabled in config.yml lacks one of the zones the flows expect, or has one turned off in Frigate (in its configuration or from its live view), because an object never enters a zone that is off. Zones are drawn in Frigate, so when one camera has the problem, its link, Edit its zones in Frigate, opens Frigate's masks and zones settings at that camera; with several, it opens the Cameras page, which links each one. The Zone names check warns when one of those cameras has a zone that is on and whose name looks like an address or a person's name, because the name is saved with every event that enters the zone. It counts the names and doesn't show them, because the diagnostics file includes the checks; the Cameras page shows which, and Zone names are saved with your data says what it looks for. The Radar names check warns when a camera is paired with a radar that is missing from sensors.radars or turned off. The camera is still recorded, but it gets no speed or direction from a radar. A radar named differently from the node-red-tm.env variables is a problem, and has no link, because you fix that name in config.yml.

The control app can't restart itself. If it stops, see If the control app is down.

docs.title: The setup history checks
docs.text:
The device records the detection model, its software versions, and each camera's settings, so a count can be tied to the setup that made it; see Setup history. Two checks watch it.

The Setup history check, in the Apps group:

Result Meaning and what to do Passed: the model, the versions, and each camera's settings are recorded A snapshot of the setup arrived in the last 15 minutes and was complete. Passed: the setup couldn't be read whole, so the recorded setup stays as it is The snapshots arrive, but one couldn't be made whole: Frigate didn't answer, is in safe mode, or didn't say which profile is active, config.yml couldn't be read, or the control app failed to gather the snapshot. Nothing was compared. Look at the Frigate check and the Node-RED configuration check. If both pass, download the diagnostics and send them with your question. When the control app itself failed, it logs The setup snapshot failed once, when the failure starts, so the line can be older than the file's last 50; the log of tm-control.service in Cockpit has it. The setup is recorded again once the snapshot can be read whole. Passed: waiting for the first snapshot Node-RED started less than 10 minutes ago. Warning: no snapshot has arrived since Node-RED started Nothing has reached Node-RED for 10 minutes. The control app sends a snapshot every five minutes, so look at the Services group for the control app, and if it stays this way, download the diagnostics. Warning: the last snapshot arrived a while ago The same, after a snapshot had arrived. Nothing is lost: the rows stay as they are, and the next snapshot brings them up to date. Warning: Node-RED's flows don't keep the setup history The flows on the device are older than the control app. Re-run the installer with tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm. Couldn't run Node-RED isn't answering, or its report of the setup history can't be read, so its state isn't known.

The Model and profile names check, in the Configuration group, warns when the running model's title, the file name of a model you uploaded (the part before its last dot), or the key of Frigate's active profile, looks like an address or a person's name. All three are saved in the database. Numbers in a title or a file name don't count: the 512 in bikes-512 is a size. The check never shows the name. For a model, Open the Detection page takes you to the Detection page, where you can use another model. For a profile, rename it in Frigate's config. It couldn't run until the control app has read the setup once.

docs.title: The Device page
docs.text: The card at the top shows the device's name, its Raspberry Pi model and memory, the Traffic Monitor version, the serial number, how long it has been running, its free storage, the processor's temperature, and the power supply's state. It also lists each connected link, Ethernet or Wi-Fi, with its IP address and MAC address, and Network details opens the Network page. If the device can't read its network state, the card leaves the list out. Software lists the versions of Frigate, Node-RED, go2rtc, nginx, and the Hailo driver if installed, the Traffic Monitor commit, the operating system, and the kernel.

docs.title: Tokens and keys
docs.text:
Administrators set the credentials the device uses for outside services in Tokens and keys. The section is closed when the page opens; select its heading to open it. It lists the Plate Recognizer API token and license key when the Plate Recognizer add-on is installed. Each is kept with the device's other secrets, not in config.yml. The ThingsBoard access token is on the Sharing page, next to the choices about what the device uploads, and the Frigate+ API key is on the Detection page, next to the models it fetches.

  • A value is never shown back. The page says whether it's set and, for a token or key of 12 or more characters, its last four characters, so you can tell which one you entered. It never shows any of the license key.
  • Save stores what you typed in the box. The eye icon shows it while you type. A Plate Recognizer value takes printable ASCII characters without spaces, up to 256 characters.
  • Remove asks first, then empties the value. Without the Plate Recognizer values plates aren't read.
  • Saving or removing restarts the app that uses the value, and the page waits for it. The license key restarts one app and takes about thirty seconds. The Plate Recognizer API token restarts the add-on and Node-RED, which takes about a minute. Traffic isn't counted while Node-RED restarts.

An older device may have kept a token in config.yml or in the add-on's env file, or a Frigate+ key in frigate.env. The installer moves it to the device's secrets, so uploads, plate reads, and Frigate+ keep working, and the Sharing page, the Device page, and the Detection page show each as set. A warning on the Status page's ThingsBoard upload check says when config.yml still holds a token key, which nothing reads, or when the upload is on without a token.

docs.title: Download diagnostics
docs.text:
When you ask for help, send the diagnostics with your question. It's a text file with the device's facts, its date and time settings, every status check, the services' states, what the installer installed and found, and the last 50 lines of each service's log. Passwords, keys, tokens, and the setup code are replaced with <redacted>. So are the names Frigate uses for cameras whenever they differ from the camera's name in config.yml, because the name in config.yml is the one the device records and shares, and Frigate's own name stays on the device. What a saved change to Frigate's settings held, such as a zone's name, is replaced too. The file still holds the device's name and serial number, the names of its Wi-Fi network and hotspot, and the user name it was installed under; replace any you don't want to share.

  • Download diagnostics saves the file.
  • Copy puts the text on the clipboard, ready to paste into a message. If the browser doesn't allow it, the page shows the text in a box, already selected, for you to copy.

The camera names replaced are Frigate's cameras that have a different name in config.yml, Frigate's cameras that no entry in config.yml points at (read from Frigate and from Frigate's own configuration file, so they are covered while Frigate isn't running), and the names found in the copies of config.yml that the control app saves beside it. It saves one each time it changes config.yml, from the Cameras page or the Location page, and keeps the last ten. A short name is replaced only when it stands alone as a word, so front is replaced in "front camera" but not in "frontage". Four limits:

  • If you renamed a camera by editing config.yml by hand, there is no saved copy with the old name. The old name can then appear in log lines from before the change, until they scroll out of the logs.
  • A short, everyday name such as front is replaced wherever that word appears in the file. That errs on the side of hiding too much.
  • On a device whose config.yml still names a camera by the name you gave it in Frigate, that name is the one the device records, so it isn't replaced. Switch the camera to a neutral name first.
  • When Frigate isn't answering and its configuration file can't be read (a YAML mistake in it, for example), a camera that has no entry in config.yml yet can't be recognized, so its name can appear in the log lines.

docs.title: Reboot or shut down
docs.text:
Reboot the device and Shut down the device each ask before they act. A reboot takes about two minutes, during which no page answers. If something such as a system update is holding the device up, or the control app isn't allowed to, the device says it can't reboot or shut down right now. Try again in a few minutes, and if it keeps happening, download the diagnostics.

Shut down only when you can reach the device

After a shutdown, nothing starts the device again from the network. To turn it back on, unplug its power and plug it back in.

docs.title: The Date and time page
docs.text:
The page shows two clocks side by side: This device and This browser (the phone or computer you're using), each with its date and offset from UTC. Under them, a sentence says whether they agree, or how far apart they are and whether their time zones differ.

  • Set from this browser sends your browser's time and time zone to the device. If the device already has its time from the internet, it keeps that time, and only the time zone changes. Otherwise it takes your browser's time. If the device doesn't know your browser's time zone, which can happen when your phone or computer has a newer list of zones, it still takes the time, leaves its time zone as it was, and asks you to pick one from the list.
  • Time zone: pick a zone, type part of its name to find it, then choose Save time zone. The installer sets the first time zone (its -z option, see Installer options); this page changes it later. The dashboards show times, and start each day at 04:00, in the device's time zone.
  • Keep time from the internet turns internet time on or off. The sentence under the switch says where the device's time comes from now.

Changing the time zone restarts Frigate, Node-RED, and the web proxy, so they all use the new zone. The page stops answering for a moment, and traffic isn't counted for about a minute.

Moving the clock ahead by more than about 20 seconds stops Frigate's camera feed, and a move of a few minutes can stop it until Frigate restarts. So when a change moves the clock ahead by that much, the device restarts Frigate and the page says so. Traffic isn't counted for about a minute. Moving the clock back restarts nothing, unless internet time briefly puts the device's later time back while it's being set, and then the page says so.

When the device has no internet

A Raspberry Pi keeps no time while it's off, unless it has a clock battery. A device without internet then starts with a clock that may be wrong. The Status page's Clock check shows a warning that no time source is reachable, or a problem if the date is before 2026. Open Date and time on your phone or computer and choose Set from this browser. The clock is usually behind after a power-off, so this moves it ahead and restarts Frigate; the camera is back in about a minute. Internet time stays on, so the device corrects its clock by itself once it's online; until then the warning stays. If the device's clock was ahead, turning internet time back on puts that wrong time back, so the device sets your time again, leaves internet time off, and the page says so. Turn on Keep time from the internet once the device is online. If that puts the wrong time back for a moment, the device restarts Frigate; the camera is back in about a minute. If a later correction stops the camera, the Status page offers Restart Frigate. A device that is never online keeps time from its own clock, which drifts; set it again now and then.

docs.title: What viewers see
docs.text:
Viewers see all five pages, and the Sharing page, but can't change anything:

  • Status: the same checks, without the Restart and Re-scan buttons.
  • Device: the card and the software versions, without Tokens and keys, Diagnostics, and Power.
  • Detection: the models and the label lists, without the action buttons and the Frigate+ key form; see Choose the detection model.
  • Date and time: the clocks, the time zone, and where the time comes from, without the button, the zone picker, or the switch.
  • Network: the addresses and the hotspot's state, without the hotspot's password or any control.
  • Sharing: what the device shares and how the server last answered, without the server's address when it's an operator's own, the token, or the form.

docs.title: description: The device's home page and the apps it links to: dashboards, Frigate, Node-RED, camera feeds, and Cockpit.
Home page and apps
docs.text:
Open http://<device>/ in a browser on the same network. <device> is the hostname you set when you imaged the card, followed by .local (for example http://tm-01.local/), or the device's IP address.

The home page is the device's control app. A new device first asks you to claim it with its setup code; after that, the home page and every app ask you to log in. The home page shows the device's name, software version, serial number, and time, a one-line summary of its health, and links to the apps your account can open. Its menu has Status, Device, and Date and time (see Check and fix the device), Network (see Wi-Fi and the hotspot), Detection (see Choose the detection model), Cameras and Location for administrators (see Cameras and Places and location), Sharing (see Share data), your Account, the Users page for administrators, About, and Log out.

Link Path What it is Who can open it Dashboard /dashboard/ The Traffic Monitor dashboards: Monitoring, Movements, and Data export, which opens first. Switch pages in the sidebar. Any user. The Data export downloads need an administrator. Frigate /frigate/ Object detection: live view, detections with snapshots and clips, zones, masks, and the Frigate settings. See Tune object detection. Any user. Frigate's settings need an administrator. Legacy Dashboard /ui/ The older dashboard, with the same counts and speed statistics as Monitoring. It's the only dashboard that shows air quality readings, and the Monitoring dashboard's counts follow its camera and radar selection. Its System Settings tab shows the device's name, time zone, and software versions. Any user Node-RED editor /nr/ The flow editor, for developers. See Dev environment. Administrators Camera feeds /feeds/ The camera streams the Pi camera produces, for checking that the camera works. It's for watching only: go2rtc's settings, stream editor, and log pages aren't available here. Administrators Cockpit http://<device>:9090/ Services, logs, containers, and a terminal. See System administration. Administrators see its link. Anyone with the Raspberry Pi user account can log in.

Cockpit is the one app with its own port. It asks for the Raspberry Pi user account, not your control app login.

docs.title: Getting back to the home page
docs.text:
Every app except Cockpit shows a small home button. Press it to come back to the home page. Viewers see it on the dashboards and Frigate. Administrators also see it on the Node-RED editor and the camera feeds.

  • Move it if it covers something: drag it to either side of the window, at any height. It settles on the nearer side.
  • Tuck it away by dragging it all the way to the left or right edge of the window and letting go there. A thin handle stays on the edge; press the handle to bring the button back. With the button selected from the keyboard, Escape tucks it.
  • Each app remembers its own spot, separately in each browser.

On a computer the button also shows the device's name. If you share a screenshot of an app and would rather the name weren't in it, tuck the button first. On a narrow screen, such as a phone held upright, the button is the icon alone.

In an Android phone's sign-in window

The window that opens when a phone joins the device's hotspot has gestures of its own: dragging down reloads the page, and a drag that starts near a side goes back or forward. So there the button is hard to move. Pressing it and tucking it still work. To place the button where you like, open the device on a laptop or desktop computer instead.

The control app's tab, from the login page on, and the tab of each app with the button start with the device's name, so you can tell several devices apart in one browser window.

Finding the device's address
  • If you set a hostname in Raspberry Pi Imager, http://<hostname>.local/ works from most computers and phones on the same network.
  • Otherwise, look the device up in your router's list of connected devices, or see Find the IP address of your Raspberry Pi.
  • A device whose Wi-Fi isn't on a network it knows runs its own hotspot. Join it, and your phone's sign-in window opens the home page; or open http://10.42.0.1/. See Wi-Fi and the hotspot.
If the home page doesn't load

Apart from Cockpit, the apps accept connections only from the device, so they have no address of their own on your network. If the apps show a page saying the control app isn't answering, restart it as described in If the control app is down. If nothing loads, open Cockpit at http://<device>:9090, log in with your Raspberry Pi user account, and check the services as described in System administration. Network ports lists what the device opens. If the home page loads on a computer but times out on an Android phone, the phone's browser needs a permission; see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Places and location
docs.text: The control app's Location page records where the device is and which way its sensors face. It also sets how precisely the database stores the location. Only the administrator sees the page, because it shows exact coordinates. A device that stays in one place works without it, so use it when you move the device, turn it, or plan to share its data.

docs.title: Places and deployments
docs.text:
A place is somewhere the device has been, is, or will be. Each place has an id such as 3f9a1c2e-si, an optional description that only you see, and an optional location, its latitude and longitude. A place doesn't need a location: a device with none still counts and records its data, only without saying where. One place can hold sensors that face different ways, such as a corner with a radar looking down each street.

One place is always In use. The others are Planned, entered ahead of a move, or Used, where the device has been. Claiming a new device creates its first place, First location, with no location.

Each sensor at a place, facing one way, for one stretch of time, is a deployment. Every count and reading is stored with its deployment, so you can tell where it was taken after the device moves. Moving to another place, or turning a sensor, starts a new deployment, and the earlier ones keep what they recorded.

The exact location is kept in the control app and in Node-RED's settings file, config.yml. The database stores the place's id and the location rounded to the precision you choose.

docs.title: The Location page
docs.text:
Location is in the control app's menu, after Cameras. The card at the top shows the place in use: its description, its id, the location as the database stores it, the exact location, what the device shares, and the way each sensor faces. Then come the list of places, the exact locations (a list and a copy of the database), and, last, the precision.

Each place in the list shows its description, or No description, its mark (In use, Planned, or Used), its id, and its location as the database stores it. Select a place to open it. An open place shows:

  • Imported from your previous settings for a place that came from an older version's data; see Update the software.
  • When the place was first and last used, or Not used yet.
  • How many events were recorded there, and between which dates.
  • Its deployments, newest first, grouped by when they were deployed: the sensors started together sit under one date, each with the way it faced and Correct heading. A radar deployed with a camera is indented under it. A sensor that ended before the rest of its group says when.
  • The buttons for what you can do with the place: Deploy here for a planned place, Re-deploy here for a used one, or Modify deployment for the place in use; Edit for a planned place; Correct location for a used place or the place in use that has a location; and Delete for any place but the one in use.

Before any place was recorded counts the deployments that had already ended when the device got its first place. They belong to no place, and the database keeps them as they are. Deployments still running then joined that first place.

If Node-RED hasn't answered yet, as right after an update, a warning at the top says past places may be missing. Reload the page once Node-RED is running. Opening the control app's home page or Status page sets the places up too.

docs.title: Add a place
docs.text:
Choose Add a place, fill in what you know, and Save. The place is added as planned.

  • Description: a name for the place, such as "Front of the school". It never leaves the device.
  • Coordinates: the latitude and longitude, pasted from a maps app as one value, such as 45.52252, -122.69120, or picked on a map. Use a dot as the decimal mark. The device keeps five decimal places, about a metre. Use at least four, about 10 metres, for an exact location: with fewer, the form warns and says how coarse the point is (about 100 metres for three decimals, and coarser for fewer), and still saves it. Leave the field empty for a place with no location.
  • Facing, for each sensor turned on in the settings: a compass point, N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, or NW, or Not set. See Which way a sensor faces.

Use this phone's location fills in the coordinates from your phone's location. Browsers share a location only with pages opened over HTTPS, and the device uses plain HTTP, so the form usually says to paste coordinates instead.

docs.title: Pick the point on a map
docs.text:
Under the coordinates, Pick on a map opens a map. Tap the spot to place a pin, drag the pin to the exact place, and choose Use this point. The form fills in the coordinates with five decimal places, and you can still change them before you save. The same button is on Correct location.

The map is drawn by your phone or computer, not by the device. It opens at the coordinates in the field, else at the place in use, else over the region of the device's time zone: a wide view around that city, about the size of a time zone. The device finds the region from its own time zone, so it asks no one, and uses it only when its Wi-Fi country is set and is one of the countries that time zone covers. Otherwise it opens on the whole world. The installer sets the time zone (its -z option, America/Los_Angeles unless you give another), so a device left on the installer's time zone and Wi-Fi country opens over Los Angeles until you set its time zone on the Date and time page. Your browser asks the map's server, named in the dialog, for the pictures of the area you look at, and the device sends it nothing. The server sees the map tiles that cover the area you look at, squares of roughly one to two kilometres across, even when you zoom in as far as the map goes. That includes the area of the place in use the moment the map opens, even when you are adding a place somewhere else. Opened over the region, the map asks for tiles that cover an area thousands of kilometres across, which says little more than your phone's internet address already does. As any website does, the server also sees your phone's internet address. It never gets the exact point you choose. If the map can't load, the dialog says so and offers Try again; type or paste the coordinates instead.

The map isn't offered while your phone is on the device's own hotspot, because the hotspot has no internet. The form says so; paste the coordinates, or open the page once the device is on your Wi-Fi.

To get coordinates from a maps app on your phone, in Google Maps press and hold the spot, then copy the coordinates shown. In Apple Maps, drop a pin; its card shows the coordinates. The phone's GPS needs no internet connection, though the app's map may not draw without one.

To change a planned place, open it and choose Edit. A place that has been used can't be edited; correct it instead.

docs.title: Which way a sensor faces
docs.text:
A sensor's heading is the way it faces, in whole degrees clockwise from true north, from 0 to 359: 0 is north, 90 is east, 180 is south, and 270 is west. The page shows it with the nearest compass point, such as NE (40°). A point covers the 45 degrees around its centre, so 23 to 67 degrees is NE, and 338 to 359 and 0 to 22 is N.

The page lets you pick one of the eight points, which sets the heading to the point's centre, as the table of centres lists. Nothing stores the point itself, only the number. A heading you measured more closely, such as 40 from a compass app, or typed into config.yml or an imported file, is kept as it is and listed first in the choices as NE (40°), so opening the choice and closing it changes nothing. Pick a point only to replace it. Until you save or close the form, the measured heading stays in the list, so you can choose it again if you picked a point by mistake.

Use true north, not magnetic north, because the two differ by several degrees in many places, and a phone's compass app can show either. A heading is optional. Not set records that you haven't said.

A device updated from an older release has its earlier headings converted; see Headings after an update.

docs.title: Move or turn the device
docs.text:
When the device moves to another place, record it from that place: Deploy here if the place is planned, or Re-deploy here if the device has been there before. When a sensor is turned to face another way, record it with Modify deployment on the place in use.

  1. Open the place, and choose its button.
  2. Check the review. For each sensor, it says whether a new deployment starts, the way the sensor faced before, and the way it faces now, which you can change. Under the sensors are what the database will store for the place and whether the device shares its data.
  3. Choose Deploy, Re-deploy, or Modify.

The page waits while Node-RED starts the new deployments, then lists their ids, each with Copy. Counts from then on belong to the new deployments.

In Modify deployment, the review starts with each sensor's heading as it is, and each sensor reads Unchanged until you change its heading. Modify stays off until at least one heading changes, and only the sensors you turned start a new deployment.

Don't deploy twice

If Node-RED hasn't loaded the new settings within about 20 seconds, the page says the settings are saved and the deployments appear once Node-RED loads them. If the connection drops while the page waits, it says the settings may already be saved. In both cases, close the dialog and check the place in the list before you deploy again.

Deploying at another place records none of a sensor's tilt, height, distance, or mount, at a place the unit was at before just as at a new one, because the unit was taken down and put up again. Modify deployment keeps them, because the unit stayed where it was. The sensors have none of the four until you record them (see How a sensor is mounted). At a place used before, the control app keeps the values last saved for each sensor there and offers them, and they are recorded when someone saves them, which for now is a save through the control app's API. There is no way to dismiss them: they are offered until a save records that sensor's mounting. A value typed into config.yml by hand isn't remembered. The heading is the one you choose in the review, which starts from the place's last one.

A move usually also needs the camera's zones adjusted; see First-time setup.

docs.title: Correct a wrong location or heading
docs.text:
A correction is for a value that was entered wrong. It changes what the records already say, and starts no new deployment. If the device moved or was turned, record that instead.

  • Correct location, on a used place or the place in use, takes a new latitude and longitude, typed or picked on a map. Every record from the place then says it was at the new point, rounded to the precision each was stored at. For the place in use, config.yml takes the new point too. A point more than about 1 km from the old one looks like a move, so the page asks a second time and gives the distance. A place with no location can't be corrected to one: add a new place with the location, and deploy it.
  • Correct heading, on each deployment in an open place, takes the way the sensor really faced, as a compass point or Not set. Every record from that deployment then says so. For a deployment that is still running, config.yml takes the new heading too.

Each correction can have a Reason, which is kept with the correction on the device. Copies of the database already downloaded, and data already uploaded, keep the old values.

docs.title: Import places from a file
docs.text:
To plan several places at once, choose Import places. Pick a CSV file, or paste its lines into the box.

  • The first line is the header. It starts with description,lat,lon, then has one column for each sensor turned on in the settings, named as in the settings. The dialog shows this device's header.
  • Each further line is one place. Leave lat and lon both empty for a place with no location. A sensor's column holds the way it faces: a compass point (n, ne, e, se, s, sw, w, or nw), a heading in whole degrees from north (0 to 359, such as 40), or nothing. A point is saved as its centre, so e is 90.
  • A file can be up to 64 KiB.

For a device with the Pi camera and one radar:

description,lat,lon,picam_h265,TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00
Front of the school,45.52252,-122.69120,n,n
Corner by the park,,,e,e

Choose Preview to see the places the file holds and, by line number, any lines with a problem. Import adds the places as planned. It's offered only when every line can be read, and it adds all of them or none.

docs.title: Delete a place
docs.text:
Open the place and choose Delete, then confirm. A planned place is removed from the list. A used place's exact location is deleted with it, and the database keeps the rounded location stored with each of its records. Deleting can't be undone.

The place in use can't be deleted. Deploy another place first.

docs.title: Export the exact locations
docs.text:
Export exact locations, above the precision, saves a CSV file with one line for each place: its id, its exact latitude and longitude (empty for a place with no location), its mark, and when it was added and last changed. It has no descriptions. Use it to match a copy of the database, which holds each place's id and rounded location, with where the device really was, for analysis and mapping.

The page asks first, because the file says exactly where the device has been, and anyone you give it to can match it to the database by place id. To get the exact locations inside a copy of the database instead, see Download the database with exact locations.

docs.title: Download the database with exact locations
docs.text:
Download the database with exact locations, next to Export exact locations, saves a copy of the database that also holds where the device was. Use it when the person who analyzes the data should map it at the real places, and a separate list of places to match by id would be one more step.

Choose the button and read the question. It says that the copy holds the exact location of each place the device has been at, that the database on the device keeps its rounded locations, and that you should give the copy only to someone who should know where the device was. Choose Download. The device makes a consistent copy of the database first, so the download starts after a wait, which can take a few minutes for a large database, and the page says so. The copy needs free space about the size of the database, as the Data export download does. If the device can't make the copy, the browser has already left the Location page and shows a plain text page with the reason instead of a file: go back to the Location page, and reload it before you try again. Once a copy has started, the button stays off until you reload the page, so that a second copy isn't started by mistake while the first is still being made.

The button is off, with the reason under it, until a place the device has been at, one marked In use or Used, has a location. A planned place doesn't count, because the device was never there.

The file is named <hostname>_<time>_tmdb-exact-locations.tar.gz and holds tmdb-exact-locations.sqlite. The name says what it is, so nobody takes it for the database you can share. On a phone joined to the unit's hotspot, see Phones for how downloads save.

docs.title: What the copy adds
docs.text:
The copy is the database as it is, with two more things in it:

  • The table survey_exact_location has one row for each place: its id, and its exact latitude and longitude.
  • The view deployment_exact is the deployment table with two more columns, exact_lat and exact_lon, from the place the row names.

The deployment table itself is not changed. Its lat and lon still hold the location rounded to the precision stored with each row, so a script that reads them gets the rounded location from every file, and an exact point can't be picked up by mistake. To list where the device was and when, with each deployment's sensor, start, end, and exact point:

SELECT sensorName,
       datetime(entryStartDateTime / 1000, 'unixepoch') AS started,
       datetime(entryEndDateTime / 1000, 'unixepoch') AS ended,
       exact_lat, exact_lon
FROM deployment_exact
ORDER BY entryStartDateTime;

The times are in UTC, and ended is empty for a deployment that is still running. A place has one exact point, so this covers every place the device has been at, past ones included, and not only the one in use.

The table holds the places the device has been at that have a location. A planned place is never in it, and neither is a place the database doesn't name. The view's exact_lat and exact_lon are empty for:

  • A place with no location.
  • A place the control app no longer has, because you deleted it.
  • A deployment from before any place was recorded, which names no place.

A correction shows in the copy as corrected: the place has one point, and a corrected place has the new one, with its rows' rounded location corrected the same way. A copy you downloaded earlier keeps the values it had, so two copies of the same device can differ, and the newer one is right. The copy doesn't hold the record of corrections.

The database on the device is unchanged: it never holds the table or the view, and the Download the database button on the Data export page still saves rounded locations only. The device removes its working copy when the download ends. The file you saved says where the device was, so give it only to people who should know. The table holds what the exact_location attribute holds when you share the exact location.

docs.title: Choose the precision
docs.text:
Precision, at the end of the page, sets how much of the location the database stores. To better protect your privacy, it's rounded to about 1 km by default. The choices stay closed until you open Change the precision, which also shows the current choice, because most devices never need to change it. The setting is for the whole device, not for one place. Each choice shows how the same point would be stored:

Choice The database stores No location stored No coordinates About 10 km (45.5, -122.7) One decimal place, about a city About 1 km (45.52, -122.69), the default Two decimal places, about a neighborhood

The exact location is never stored in the database. It stays on this device, and leaves it only if you share it, export it, download a copy of the database that holds it, or save it with a camera's reference picture. Choose one and Save.

  • A coarser choice applies to the deployments running now at once. Rows stored before them keep their precision unless you tick Also round the rows already stored, which asks first, because it can't be undone.
  • No location stored removes the stored location from the deployments running now at once. Tick Also remove it from the rows already stored to remove it from every row in the database as well, which also asks first. The exact location stays on the device, but the database can't get the rounded values back.
  • A finer choice applies from the next deployment. Rows already stored stay as they are, because what was rounded away can't come back.

docs.title: What leaves the device
docs.text:
• A place's description, and the reasons you give for corrections, never leave the device.
  • A copy of the database holds the place's id and its location at the stored precision: about a neighborhood at about 1 km, or about a city at about 10 km. The exact location isn't in it, unless you made the copy with Download the database with exact locations, which adds each place's exact location in a table of its own.
  • Data you share carries the location as the database stores it. The exact location goes only if you tick Share the exact location, and only for the place in use. The file from Export exact locations, and the copy from Download the database with exact locations, go where you send them.
  • A camera's reference picture holds the exact location of the place in use unless you clear Include this place's exact location, and the pictures show the street. The zip goes where you send it.
  • A correction or a coarser precision changes the device's own records only. Copies of the database already downloaded, and data already uploaded, keep the values they had.

To change these values in config.yml by hand, see Edit the location by hand.

docs.title: Share data
docs.text: A Traffic Monitor shares nothing until an administrator turns it on. The control app's Sharing page, in its menu, sets where the device uploads its data and what goes with it. Everyone who is logged in can see what the device shares and how the server last answered. Only the administrator can change anything.

docs.title: Choose the server
docs.text:
Server What differs Traffic Monitor's server The default. Before you turn sharing on, or add a choice to it, you read the notice that says what is done with the data. The public map choice is offered only for this server. Your own ThingsBoard server You give its host, its protocol (https or http), and, if it isn't on the standard port, its port. The notice and the public map don't apply to it. Once data leaves the device, it's your responsibility to make that server honour the choices you make on this page.

Changing the server turns off the exact location and the public map. Each choice is given for one server, so tick them again for the new one.

docs.title: Set the access token
docs.text:
The server gives each device an access token. Enter it in Access token and choose Save token. The page says whether a token is set and its last four characters, and never shows it back. A token takes letters, digits, and . _ ~ -, and is up to 256 characters long.

Saving the token restarts Node-RED, which takes about thirty seconds. The device counts nothing while it restarts. Share data can't be ticked until a token is set.

docs.title: Choose what the device shares
docs.text:
Each of the three choices starts off, is ticked on its own, and is turned off in the same place: untick it and choose Save. See an example under each one shows what is sent, with made-up values.

Choice What it sends What it doesn't send Share data Each event with its speed and direction, its path across the camera's picture, its box, and how long it stood still and spent in each zone, the radar and air quality readings, every five minutes whether each camera and radar was working (the watch log), and the device's system health: its software versions, name on the network, time zone, serial number, temperature, and disk use. With them goes where the device is, as the database stores it: the place's id and its location rounded to about 1 km, unless you chose another precision, and how each sensor is mounted: the way it faces and, when you have recorded them, its tilt, height, the distance to the centre of its view, and its usual mount. Only the fields on the list of what is shared are sent, so any other column of a deployment stays on the device. Turning this off stops every upload. Images, video, plate reads, the device's settings, its Wi-Fi details, and the descriptions you give places. Share the exact location The exact coordinates of the place in use, with its id. For Traffic Monitor's server, the notice says how they are used; for your own server, that is up to whoever runs it. It needs Share data, and over your own server it needs https. Nothing is sent until the place in use has a location. Any place but the one in use. Show this device on the public map A point rounded to about 100 m, and nothing else about where the device is. It needs Share data, and it's offered for Traffic Monitor's server only. The box says Not live yet until a release opens the map. The exact location.

For Traffic Monitor's server, the page requires you to read the notice, and to tick I've read the notice, when a save turns Share data on, switches to Traffic Monitor's server, or adds a choice under a notice that has changed. A save that only keeps or turns off choices never requires it. When the notice changes, the device keeps sharing as you set it, and, while Share data is on, the page offers I've read the notice until someone ticks it and saves. Ticking it and choosing Save records your choices under the new version, and the Status page stops asking. A choice you add after the change waits for you to read it.

The exact location is for you to give or keep

The database stores the location rounded, so a shared copy of the database carries the rounded location only. The exact location leaves the device only under Share the exact location, or in what you save from the Location page: the file from Export exact locations, or the copy of the database from Download the database with exact locations. You give those yourself, and nothing is sent.

docs.title: What the server already has
docs.text: Turning a choice off stops the device sending. What the server already received stays there. To ask for it to be deleted, use the email address in the notice (for Traffic Monitor's server) or ask the operator of your own server.

docs.title: Check that the server gets the data
docs.text:
The Server status line on the Sharing page, and the Sharing server check in the Apps group of the Status page, say how the server last answered. The device checks again after a save while it waits for the first upload. The control app never contacts the server itself: Node-RED records how each upload went.

Status Meaning and what to do Off Nothing is uploaded. Waiting for the first upload Sharing is on and no upload has been sent since the settings loaded. The device sends system health every five minutes. Accepted an upload 4 minutes ago The server is taking the data. No upload accepted for a while The server hasn't accepted an upload for more than 15 minutes. Check the device's internet connection on the Network page. Can't be reached The device couldn't reach the server. The device keeps counting and recording, and an upload that fails isn't sent again, so the server misses what the device sent while it was offline. This is a warning, because an offline device is normal. Refused the token The server doesn't accept this device's token. The Status page's Check the token link opens the token's section. This is a problem. Refused an upload The server turned down what the device sent. Ask the server's operator. This is a problem. Answered with an error The server had an error. This is a warning; it usually passes. If it doesn't, ask the operator. Not known Node-RED isn't answering, so the status isn't known. See the Node-RED check in the Apps group.

The Sharing check, in the Configuration group, says what is shared: Not sharing, Sharing data, or Sharing data and the exact location, and whether the public map is on. It's a warning, with a Review sharing link, when the page needs a look: after an update, when no one has read the notice yet or it has changed, or when the sharing block in config.yml has a value the device ignores. Opening the Sharing page and choosing Save rewrites that block.

docs.title: After an update
docs.text:
A device that already uploaded before it had these choices keeps uploading, with the location as the database stores it. The exact location stops until an administrator turns it on.
