The first time someone opens the Status, Location, or Sharing page, the control app adds a sharing block to config.yml that records this, with the exact location and the public map both off. Node-RED reloads its settings once when that happens. The Status page shows Review sharing until an administrator chooses I've reviewed this on the Sharing page or saves the page. Until an administrator ticks I've read the notice and saves the page, the Sharing check also says so.

The upload of the device's settings, and the Backup & Restore section of the legacy dashboard, are removed while they are reworked.

An old config.yml that still has the placeholder server tb.server.com, with the upload off, gets Traffic Monitor's server when the installer runs.

docs.title: What the installer's -f does to sharing
docs.text: Running the installer with -f writes a fresh config.yml with the upload off and no sharing block, so every choice is turned off, and none is restored afterwards. The access token stays, because the device keeps it with its other secrets. Turning the upload back on by editing the file shares the rounded data only, whether or not anyone opened a page in between: the exact location and the public map are never turned on from the file. The control app then writes the sharing block back with both turned off. Choose them again on this page.

docs.title: Where it's stored
docs.text: The page writes the server and the choices to config.yml, and keeps a record of each choice, with when it was made and which notice it was under, in the control app's own database. The config.yml copy is what Node-RED reads, so a choice you make by editing the file has no effect.

docs.title: Cockpit
docs.text:
Cockpit is the device's system console in the browser. It shows the services and their logs, the Podman containers, system updates, and the user accounts, and it has a terminal, so most administration needs no SSH client.

Open http://<device>:9090/, with the same name or address you use for the home page, and log in with your Raspberry Pi user account. Administrators also have a Cockpit tile on the home page, which opens the same address and names the account to log in with.

Cockpit has its own port and its own login. It doesn't need the home page, the control app, or the apps, so it still opens when they don't. Use it when:

  • the home page doesn't load, or a page says the control app isn't answering
  • you want to restart a service, or read its log
  • you need a terminal and have no SSH client
  • you want to install system updates or change the system password

Who can open Cockpit

Anyone on your network can reach Cockpit's login page. Only the Raspberry Pi user account gets past it. The control app's accounts don't work there.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
The Traffic Monitor runs as systemd services. The app containers run inside one Podman pod. nginx and the control app run on the host, outside the pod, so the home page and the login stay up when the pod is down.

Start with the control app's Status page: it shows each service's state, and when one has stopped or keeps failing, its check has a Restart button. Use Cockpit or SSH for the rest, such as restarting the control app itself, or a service that looks running but misbehaves.

Service What it runs traffic-monitor.service The pod that holds Frigate, Node-RED, and Plate Recognizer if installed frigate.service Frigate, object detection node-red-tm.service Node-RED: the Traffic Monitor logic, dashboards, database, and MQTT broker tm-control.service The control app: the home page's data, the login, the device's accounts, and the status checks. nginx asks it to check the login for every app. revproxy.service nginx, which serves the home page and the /dashboard/, /frigate/, and other paths plate-recognizer.service The optional Plate Recognizer add-on go2rtc_server.service go2rtc, which reads the Pi camera and streams it to Frigate. It runs on the host, not in the pod.

Over SSH:

sudo systemctl status traffic-monitor.service   # or any service above
sudo systemctl restart node-red-tm.service      # after editing node-red-tm.env
sudo journalctl -u frigate.service -f           # follow a service's log
sudo podman ps                                  # running containers

docs.title: When to restart what
docs.text: After you Do this Edit Node-RED's config.yml Nothing. The Traffic Monitor reads the file again when you save it. If the change doesn't show, check the file for a YAML error. For the location, use the control app's Location page instead; Edit the location by hand says what a hand edit does. Edit node-red-tm.env sudo systemctl restart node-red-tm.service. The container reads the file only when it starts. Edit frigate.env sudo systemctl restart frigate.service. Change the MQTT broker login in node-red-tm.env bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm. A restart isn't enough; Env file settings explains why. Rename a camera in Frigate Choose Save & Restart in Frigate's config editor, then point the camera's entry at the new name on the Cameras page. Change Frigate's config in its UI Choose Save & Restart in Frigate's config editor, or restart frigate.service. Plug in a radar Rerun the installer for Node-RED so the radar is passed to the container: bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm. Add or change an AI accelerator Rerun the installer with -t detectors -t frigate, then update Frigate's detector settings. See Add an accelerator later. See a page saying the control app isn't answering sudo systemctl restart tm-control.service, or restart it in Cockpit on port 9090. See If the control app is down. Move the device to a new site Choose Deploy here on the new place on the Location page, then adjust the zones as in First-time setup.

docs.title: The device's card
docs.text: sudo tm-control card prints the device's address, the name and password of its hotspot, and its setup code while it's unclaimed. It needs sudo because the code is in a file only root can read, and the password in a file only root and the installing user's group can. sudo tm-control card --json prints the same values as JSON. If you lose the administrator's password, sudo tm-control reset-admin starts the accounts over; see If the administrator's password is lost.

docs.title: Where things are
docs.text:
The settings and data live under /opt/traffic-monitor/.

Path Contents node-red-tm/config/config.yml Traffic Monitor settings. See config.yml settings. node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env Radar ports, database path, MQTT broker. See Env file settings. node-red-tm/db/tmdb.sqlite The database. db/backup/ holds the copy saved before the most recent schema change. After the upgrade that rounded the stored coordinates, that copy still has the exact ones, so don't share it. frigate/config/config.yml Frigate's settings, including zones and masks. frigate/config/model_cache/ The models Frigate runs, such as a Frigate+ model's two files. The control app's Detection page uploads, downloads, and deletes them. frigate/frigate.env Frigate's environment, including the Frigate+ API key, which comes from the device's secrets. See Env file settings. frigate/storage/ Frigate's snapshots and recordings. plate-recognizer/plate-recognizer.env Plate Recognizer settings, if the add-on is installed. Its token and license key come from the device's secrets, which you set on the Device page.

The control app and the installer keep a few files elsewhere. Read them, but don't edit them.

Path Contents /var/lib/tm-control/state.sqlite The control app's accounts, the license acceptance, and a log of account changes. Only the control app writes it. /etc/traffic-monitor/manifest.json What the installer installed and found, which the control app reads /etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/ Passwords and keys the installer generated on the device, including the hotspot's password, which administrators can show on the Network page, and the tokens and keys you enter on the Device page, the Detection page, and the Sharing page /etc/traffic-monitor/setup-code The setup code, until the device is claimed

docs.title: Wi-Fi and the hotspot
docs.text:
When a Traffic Monitor's Wi-Fi isn't on a network it knows, the unit runs a hotspot of its own. The hotspot is how you reach a unit at the roadside, where there's no router. It runs whether or not the unit is also on Ethernet.

The hotspot's name is TM- and four characters from the unit's serial number, such as TM-4F2A, until an administrator renames it. It uses WPA2 on the 2.4 GHz band. The Status page shows its state.

docs.title: Join the hotspot
docs.text:
1. Find the hotspot's name and password on the unit's card. The card is the printout that came with a pre-built unit; for a unit you installed yourself, the installer shows it at the end of its run on the device. An administrator can also show the password on the Network page, and sudo tm-control card on the unit prints it again, together with the setup code while the unit is unclaimed.
  2. On your phone, join the hotspot with that password. Your phone may say the network has no internet. Stay connected.
  3. The phone's sign-in window opens the control app by itself, on its login or setup page. If it doesn't, open http://10.42.0.1/ in a browser. The unit's .local name, http://<hostname>.local/, also works. On a phone, a browser needs the steps under Phones first.

The hotspot has no internet, and a phone on it reaches only the unit. Nothing on the unit's Ethernet or home network is reachable from the hotspot.

docs.title: Phones
docs.text:
The sign-in window opens the control app with nothing to set up, but it can't save every download. A browser can. The note at the top of the login and setup pages lists the steps: copy the unit's address, keep the network, and open the address in a browser.

  • Android 17:
    • To keep the network, open the sign-in window's menu and choose Use this network as is. Until you do, a phone with mobile data on doesn't use the hotspot for its browsers, so neither the unit's name nor http://10.42.0.1/ opens. Logging in to the control app in the sign-in window doesn't change that.
    • Allow Nearby devices for the browser; the Android entry has the steps. Without it the browser times out on the unit, on the hotspot and on your home network.
    • In the sign-in window, the database and JSON downloads on the Data export page save. The unit prepares the database twice there, once for the window and once for the phone's downloader, so the wait before a database download starts is about double.
    • Download the database with exact locations on the Location page saves from the sign-in window too. The phone asks for it twice, so the unit makes the copy twice and needs free space for two copies of the database for a while.
    • Download diagnostics on the Device page and Save the zip of a camera's reference picture don't save from the sign-in window: the phone says "Could not download". The reference pictures themselves do show there. Both save from a browser.
    • Frigate's downloads, such as a snapshot, don't save from the sign-in window either.
  • iPhone: to stay on the hotspot and save downloads, tap Cancel on the sign-in sheet and choose Use Without Internet. Then open http://10.42.0.1/ or the unit's .local name in a browser. Without that choice the iPhone goes back to another network it knows, and a download in progress is cut off. The sign-in sheet itself shows a downloaded file's contents instead of saving it.

The Location page's map needs the internet, so the page doesn't offer it on the hotspot. Paste the coordinates there, or open the page once the device is on your Wi-Fi.

Tested with a Pixel 7 on Android 17 (the sign-in window, Chrome, and Firefox) and with Firefox on an iPhone on iOS 18.7, in November 2026.

docs.title: The Network page
docs.text:
Network in the control app's menu shows how to reach the unit and what it is connected to. Everyone who is signed in sees:

  • This device: the unit's name and its .local name, such as tm-ab12 and tm-ab12.local.
  • Ethernet and Wi-Fi: whether each is connected, and for each its MAC address, IP address, gateway, and DNS servers. The Wi-Fi line says which network the unit is on, with its signal, or that it is on its own hotspot. A unit without Ethernet has no Ethernet line, and a unit without a built-in radio says so.
  • Internet: whether the unit reaches the internet. An offline unit says Not reachable, which is normal.
  • Hotspot: whether it is on, its name, whether the name is hidden, and the two addresses it answers on.
  • Wi-Fi networks: the networks the unit has saved and the ones it heard the last time it looked. See Put the unit on a Wi-Fi network and Saved networks.

This device and Hotspot sit side by side on a wide screen, above Wi-Fi networks, and are folded each time you open the page. Folded, This device shows the .local name and the addresses in use, and Hotspot shows its name, or Hotspot off. Select a heading to open it. While the unit is on a Wi-Fi network and the hotspot is on, a grey line under the hotspot's name says the hotspot is only a fallback and names that network, and the open panel starts with a sentence on when the hotspot would start; see When the hotspot runs. A panel opens by itself when something in it needs your attention, such as a hotspot change that fails or is refused, and a folded one then shows a warning mark.

Every name and address has a Copy button. If the network service doesn't answer, the page says so and shows only the names.

The Device page shows the same addresses in a short summary, with a link to this page.

Find the MAC address

A router set to admit listed devices only needs the unit's Wi-Fi MAC address. Open This device on the Network page, copy the address from the Wi-Fi block, and add it to the router's list.

Viewers see the lists of networks, a join's progress card (read only, with no buttons), the hotspot's state, name, whether the name is hidden, and addresses, and nothing else. They never see its password or a control. Administrators get the controls described in the rest of this page: put the unit on a Wi-Fi network, change the saved networks, show or change the hotspot's password, rename the hotspot, hide its name, and turn it on or off.

Changes restart the hotspot

A change to the hotspot's name, password, or hidden setting restarts it when it is up. Phones on it are disconnected, and each phone must rejoin by hand. When you use the Network page from a phone on the hotspot, the page stops answering when you save. Join the hotspot again, then reload the page. The page warns you before a change that restarts the hotspot, before you turn the hotspot off, and before you hide its name. Turning the hotspot on doesn't ask.

docs.title: Put the unit on a Wi-Fi network
docs.text:
An administrator can put the unit on a Wi-Fi network from the Network page, without a cable or a keyboard. The unit tests the network first, and switches to it only once the test has passed and the countdown has ended or you choose Switch now.

  1. Open Network. Under Wi-Fi networks, choose Refresh to have the unit look for networks. It takes about 4 seconds, and a phone on the hotspot pauses for a few seconds while the unit looks. Nearby networks lists what it heard, strongest first, and says how long ago it looked.
  2. Choose Join next to the network, and read what the dialog says will happen. It shows the unit's Wi-Fi MAC address too.
  3. Type the network's password, and choose Test and join. The page shows the password as you type it, and asks only once.

The unit doesn't save the network or its password at this point. Until the switch, the network exists only in the unit's memory, so a wrong password never reaches the microSD card.

docs.title: The test
docs.text:
A test takes up to about a minute, and the unit's radio is busy with it. If the unit was on its hotspot, the hotspot is away for the test and a phone on it is disconnected. The hotspot is back within a few seconds after the test ends. Join it again by hand, and reload the page to see the result. If the unit was on another network, it leaves that network for the test and returns to it. Until the join ends (the test, the countdown, and the switch), the unit refuses every other Wi-Fi or hotspot change. Once the test has passed, choose Cancel or Switch now to free it.

The test asks the network for an address, then asks the network's DNS server for the address of connectivity-check.ubuntu.com (up to three times, a second apart, because the first question right after joining can fail) and makes one request to it, to see whether the internet is reachable. The unit comes back to where it was either way. To test a network the unit has saved already, choose Join and keep its saved password, or enter a new one.

A card at the top of the Network page shows the test as it runs. Administrators also see a line with a See it link on the home page, so you can find the result from there.

docs.title: The result and the countdown
docs.text:
When the test passes, the card says <name> works and shows:

  • the address the unit got on that network, and its .local name, which you can use to reach it there;
  • the unit's Wi-Fi MAC address;
  • whether the internet is reachable there.

Below that, a countdown starts at 5 minutes: Joining <name> in 4:32. Use the time to join the same network with your phone or computer, so you can open one of the addresses once the unit has switched.

  • Switch now ends the countdown, and the unit joins at once.
  • Cancel ends it, and the unit stays where it is. Nothing is saved.
  • If you do nothing, the unit joins when the countdown ends.

When the unit joins, the network is saved and the unit uses it. If the unit was on the hotspot, the hotspot stops. A phone on the hotspot loses it, so join the network yourself and open one of the addresses from the card. On an Android 17 phone, a browser needs the Nearby devices permission to open it; see the Android entry if the address doesn't open. The result stays on the page until you choose Dismiss.

A network with a sign-in page

Some networks, such as a hotel's or a cafe's, give the unit an address but make a device open a web page before it reaches the internet. The unit can't complete that page. The card says "Joined, but this network needs a sign-in page, so the unit has no internet there." The unit can still join the network and be reached on it, and you can switch to it if you want that.

docs.title: If the test fails
docs.text:
The card says why, and the unit is back where it was. Nothing is saved for a new network.

The card says What it means <name> isn't in range right now, so nothing was tried The unit didn't hear the network when it checked, so it left its radio alone. Choose Refresh and try again from a place with a better signal. The unit couldn't join <name> Usually a wrong password. This fails after about 25 seconds. A router set to admit listed devices only also refuses the unit until you add the unit's Wi-Fi MAC address, which the card and the dialog show, to its list. <name> let the unit in but gave it no address The unit connected, but the network's DHCP gave it nothing. This fails after about 45 seconds. Try again later, or check the network's address range. The unit was busy with its Wi-Fi Another Wi-Fi change was under way. Try again in a minute. The test couldn't run The unit couldn't prepare to come back, so it left its radio alone, or it hit an error it didn't expect. It is back where it was. The test of <name> was interrupted The test stopped partway, for example because the unit lost power. The unit goes back to where it was within a minute and a half. The test passed, but the unit couldn't join <name> when the countdown ended The unit is back where it was. If the network went away during the countdown, the switch waits for it, and the hotspot is away for up to about a minute before it comes back. The network stays saved, and the unit tries it again by itself, after a wait that grows to about an hour. See When the hotspot runs.

A saved network that fails is kept, because the cause may be temporary. A new network that fails is not saved.

docs.title: Saved networks
docs.text:
Saved networks lists the networks the unit joins by itself. Above the list the page says: "The unit joins the first of these it finds." The order is the order the unit tries them in, so the network at the top wins when more than one is in range. A network the unit joined from the page goes to the top of the list.

Each network shows whether it is Joined, In range, or Not in range, and flags a network that is Hidden or Not joined by itself. A network saved through Raspberry Pi Imager's Wi-Fi settings shows here too, as an ordinary saved network.

  • Move up and Move down change a network's place in the order. Only the networks the unit joins by itself have a place.
  • Forget deletes a saved network, after a question. The unit no longer joins it. When it isn't the network in use, nothing else changes.
  • Forget on the network in use makes the unit leave it. The question says so, and says what happens next. The hotspot starts within about 5 seconds, and a page opened over that network loses the unit, so join the hotspot and open http://10.42.0.1/. With the hotspot turned off, the question warns that the unit then has no wireless way in, and that you would need an Ethernet cable.

docs.title: Couldn't join
docs.text: A saved network that the unit failed to join shows Couldn't join. The unit tries again by itself, about 10 minutes after the failure, then about 20, then about 65 minutes after each further one; When the hotspot runs has the details. Joining the network by hand from the page, with the right password, tests it again at once.

docs.title: When the hotspot runs
docs.text:
The hotspot yields to the networks the unit has saved. A unit joins a saved network that's in range, and the hotspot runs when none is.

Situation What happens The unit starts with a saved network in range It's on the network within a minute. The hotspot stays off. The unit starts with no saved network in range The hotspot is up about 15 seconds after the unit starts. The unit's Wi-Fi network disappears The hotspot starts about 75 seconds later. A saved network has the wrong password The hotspot is away for about a minute while the unit tries the network, then comes back. You join a network from the page The hotspot is away for up to a minute for the test, then comes back. When the countdown ends, or you choose Switch now, the unit joins the network and the hotspot stops at once. You forget the network in use The hotspot starts within about 5 seconds.

While the hotspot is up and nobody is joined to it, the unit looks for its saved networks every 5 minutes and joins one it hears. A network that won't join is tried again about 10 minutes after the failure, then about 20 minutes after the next one, then about 65 minutes after each further failure. While a phone is joined to the hotspot, the unit doesn't look, so nothing interrupts the phone.

The Status page's Hotspot check says which of these the unit is in, and its Restart the hotspot button has the unit look at its radio at once.

docs.title: Turn the hotspot off
docs.text:
1. Sign in as an administrator and open Network.
  2. Under Hotspot, switch off Hotspot on.
  3. Read the warning, and choose Turn off if you still want to.

The warning says: "With the hotspot off, this unit has no wireless way in when its Wi-Fi network is missing. You would need an Ethernet cable." The hotspot stops now and doesn't start by itself again, and phones on it are disconnected. To turn it on again, switch Hotspot on back on. The unit then starts the hotspot as the table above describes; a unit that is on a saved network starts it when that network is lost.

docs.title: The password
docs.text:
The installer makes the password on the unit, at random, when it sets up the hotspot. It's twelve letters and digits in three groups, such as ABCD-EFGH-JKLM, and it's different on every unit. It never comes from the serial number, so knowing the name tells nobody the password.

The unit keeps it in /etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/hotspot_password, readable only by root and the installing user's group (tmadmin unless you installed with -g). The installer shows the card on the terminal and keeps the password out of its log; a run from another computer with -H prints only a reminder of the command.

docs.title: Show the password
docs.text:
On the Network page, an administrator opens Hotspot and chooses Show next to Password. The page asks the unit for the password each time and forgets it again when you choose Hide, change anything, or leave the page. The control app records each time an administrator shows it.

If you can't sign in, run sudo tm-control card on the unit instead. Over Ethernet or SSH works when you're locked out of the hotspot.

docs.title: Change the password
docs.text:
1. Sign in as an administrator and open Network, then open Hotspot.
  2. Next to Password, choose Change. A unit whose hotspot has no password offers Set a password here.
  3. Type the new password, 8 to 63 letters, digits, and symbols with no space at either end.
  4. Write the password down, then choose Change password, or Set password on a unit that has none.

The hotspot restarts with the new password, and phones on it are disconnected. Each phone must rejoin by hand, with the new password. The page types the password in the open and asks for it only once, so you see what you write down.

docs.title: For sellers
docs.text:
sudo tm-control card --json prints the card's values as JSON, for a label or a packing slip:

{
  "hostname": "tm-01",
  "local_url": "http://tm-01.local/",
  "hotspot": {"name": "TM-4F2A", "password": "ABCD-EFGH-JKLM", "url": "http://10.42.0.1/"},
  "claimed": false,
  "setup_code": "ABCD-EFGH"
}

setup_code is null once the unit is claimed. The command needs sudo, and it prints to the terminal only. Nothing stores or logs the card, so don't paste the output where others can read it.

docs.title: Rename the hotspot or hide its name
docs.text: An administrator can change the name phones see, and hide it, in the Hotspot panel of the Network page.

docs.title: Rename the hotspot
docs.text:
1. Open Network, open Hotspot, and next to its Name, choose Change.
  2. Type the new name. It takes 1 to 32 bytes, so fewer characters if it has accents or emoji, with no space at either end.
  3. Choose Change name.

The hotspot restarts, and each phone must join the new name by hand. A printed card still shows the old name. sudo tm-control card shows the new one.

docs.title: Hide the name
docs.text:
1. Open Network, open Hotspot, and switch on Hide the name.
  2. Read the warning, and choose Hide the name.

The warning says: "The hotspot is still on and can still be found by scanning. Only its name is hidden." Hiding the name doesn't stop anyone from finding the hotspot, so it isn't a lock. A phone no longer lists the hotspot by name. On Android, add the network by hand: choose Add network, type the name and the password, and tick Hidden network. Without that, the phone never connects. Switch Hide the name off to show the name again.

docs.title: A hotspot you set up by hand
docs.text:
A hotspot you made yourself in NetworkManager is kept. When a unit has no profile named tm-hotspot, the installer takes over your access-point profile, the one that starts by itself and was used last, renames it tm-hotspot, and stops any other access point from starting. Its name on air, password, band, and hidden setting stay as you set them. The installer sets the profile's address to 10.42.0.1 and its priority below your saved networks, and copies the password into the password file.

A hand-made hotspot with no password shows as a problem on the Status page, because anyone nearby can join it. The Status page's Set a password link opens the Network page with Hotspot open. There, next to Password, choose Set a password and follow the steps in Change the password. The installer then keeps the profile's password the same as the password file's. An empty file tells the installer to leave the hotspot's security alone.

A hand-made hotspot with a hidden name keeps it. Manage it as in Hide the name.

docs.title: Who can see the hotspot
docs.text: A hotspot on a pole is visible to anyone passing, and public Wi-Fi maps record where names are seen. The name TM- and four characters shows that a Traffic Monitor is nearby and doesn't say where it is. Hiding the name makes the hotspot harder to spot in a list, but a scan still finds it. Only turning the hotspot off prevents it, with the cost described in Turn the hotspot off. The password is what keeps people out of the control app. Control app and login explains what its login protects.

docs.title: The Wi-Fi country
docs.text:
Wi-Fi rules differ by country, and a radio with no country set uses limited worldwide settings. The installer asks for the country, as a two-letter code such as US or GB, when the unit has none. Press Enter to accept US. With -y, it keeps the unit's country, or sets US when there is none. To set it without being asked, or to change it, run the installer with -w:

bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t wifi -w GB

The change applies at once, with no reboot. The Status page warns while no country is set.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The page can't join an open network, a hidden network (a saved hidden network included), a WPA3-only network, or a network that asks for a user name as well as a password (an enterprise network). It lists open, WPA3-only, enterprise, and other kinds with the reason, such as "Open networks can't be joined." or "This kind of network can't be joined." A hidden network is never listed by a scan, and a saved hidden network shows a Hidden mark and has no Join. A network that offers both WPA2 and WPA3 is joined as WPA2. The page doesn't complete a sign-in page, it only reports one.
  • One join (the test, the countdown, and the switch) runs at a time, and the page joins over IPv4 only.
  • A network the unit is also connected to that uses 10.42.0.x addresses clashes with the hotspot's fixed address. Give that network another range.
  • The hotspot runs on the built-in radio, wlan0. If a USB Wi-Fi adapter takes that name, the hotspot stays off, and the Status page says so. Unplug the adapter and reboot.
